before: On entering the small but beautiful bay of Machico, one sees on the left, leaning out over the ocean, a chapel dedicated to São Roque (St Roch), at the foot of which lies the well-known spring of the same name. The present chapel is not the original one, which stood a short distance from it, roughly on the square that lies there, overlooking the sea. That building was old, but we do not know the year of its foundation. As it had fallen into an advanced state of ruin, its confraternity had it rebuilt in 1739, and it was then erected on the spot where it stands today. The licence granted for its blessing is dated 6 June of that year, but the date 1751 can be read on the high altar; this perhaps refers to the installation of that altar in place of another that may have stood there. Inside, the chapel is adorned with exquisite *azulejos* (painted glazed tiles) depicting the principal episodes in the life of the saint. They have been admired by Portuguese and foreigners alike, and they truly deserve a visit. A fine road leads from the centre of the town (*vila*) to the churchyard of the chapel; in the summer season it is much frequented by the holidaymakers who spend the hot months in Machico.

before: Because of its small area and small population, the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) has always formed a single parish (*freguesia*). It has borne, and still bears today, the name of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity), the patron saint of its parish church. Although Frutuoso stated in 1590 that the patron saint and name of the parish was the Salvador (the Saviour), the truth is that documents earlier than that date already give the patron saint as Nossa Senhora da Piedade, and we believe it was never any other.

before: We believe that the seat of the parish was established in the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity), which already stood there before the parish was created. It underwent various repairs and extensions, and was completely rebuilt around 1667. Nothing remains of the original building except the so-called chapel of the Morgada, which belonged to an old Baião family. It still keeps its pointed arch, which, since some of the stones forming it were somewhat damaged, was rendered with a cement coating a few years ago! No church in the diocese ever suffered so many profanations and outrages as this one, owing to the raids that corsairs made on that island from time to time. As there were no defences of any kind there, the inhabitants thought only of taking refuge on the Pico do Castelo (‘castle peak’) and in other safe places whenever they sensed the pirates approaching, leaving them a free hand to carry out their work of destruction and plunder. In 1617 Porto Santo was invaded by Algerian corsairs, and the mother church (*igreja matriz*) was sacked and set on fire; the same happened again in 1667, after which the church was rebuilt. In 1556, 1690 and 1708 it was not Moors but French ships fitted out as privateers that attacked the island and thoroughly plundered it, the parish church again being a target of the attackers’ fury. It should be remembered that in those times French ships were protected by high-ranking personages – some even claim by the kings of France themselves. These ships often roamed the seas as pirates, committing the gravest crimes with impunity, slaughtering and robbing defenceless settlements. Such was the case with the French invasion of Madeira in 1556, as we shall see in its proper place.

before: There Esmeraldo built a chapel dedicated to the Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit), also called the chapel of the Conceição (‘Conception’), which was consecrated by Bishop João Lobo in 1508 and became the seat of this entailed estate. The present church is a rebuilding from the first half of the 18th century, and it is the largest, most elegant and richest chapel in the whole diocese. Worthy of admiration and esteem is the dado of *azulejos* (painted glazed tiles) lining the lower part of the chapel’s interior walls, which depicts in symbolic figures the Gifts and the Fruits of the Holy Spirit. It has five altars and contains several exquisitely carved images. Nearby stands the vast, ruined manor house, once the most splendid country house in Madeira, rebuilt around 1679 by Luís Esmeraldo de Atouguia, holder of the entail. The last representative of this entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) was the 2nd Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), who displayed there the brilliance and magnificence with which he used to adorn his dazzling and lavish festivities. In this locality (*sítio*), at the place called Passo (‘pass’), are one of the two parish cemeteries and the ruins of an old chapel dedicated to Santo Amaro (St Maurus), whose construction is likewise attributed to João Esmeraldo. See *A Lombada dos Esmeraldos na Ilha da Madeira* by Father Fernando A. Silva.

before: The stretch of Rua dos Murças between the Avenida de João Gonçalves Zarco and the Largo da Sé was called Rua do Capitão, a name it kept until not so many years ago. In earlier times the whole of Rua dos Murças was known as Rua do Capitão. Frutuoso says: ‘From this Rua do Sabão there rises one that is called do Capitam, because it is the most direct way to his house....’ The captain to whom the *Saudades* refer was the captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, who had his residence in the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence).

before: Yet another weighty reason counsels and urges this: its venerable antiquity. Contrary to what the author of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) and his learned commentator asserted, when they named the church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*) and the chapel of São Sebastião (St Sebastian) on the Largo do Chafariz (‘fountain square’) as the first chapels built on Madeira, it is now known, without fear of serious contradiction, that the little shrine of Santa Catarina was the first church raised on this island, as we already stated more than twenty years ago in the pages of the *Elucidário Madeirense*. This acknowledged priority should be regarded as yet another irrefutable claim on our heartfelt veneration and on our ardent support for the preservation and, where possible, the embellishment of so ancient and significant a monument. We believe that a stone inscription should be placed on one of the interior walls of the tiny church, bearing these or similar words: ‘This chapel, founded by the wife of João Gonçalves Zargo, was the first built on Madeira and recalls the discovery of this island and the beginning of its settlement.’

before: It seems to have begun as a *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) under the name of Santa Teresa de Jesus, whose inmates followed the Third Order of Carmel and entered it in the year 1652. Only in 1660 was it turned into a convent, under the Franciscan rule of St Clare. Its first abbess was a nun from the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), chosen by the ecclesiastical authority. It was in that same year of 1660, that is, two years before his death, that Canon Calaça de Viveiros gave all his property to the convent he had founded. The convent and church underwent major repairs around the middle of the 18th century, when a new and spacious choir was built to replace the old one, which was cramped. The Royal Treasury (*Fazenda Real*) contributed one *conto* (one million réis) de réis to these works, as granted by the royal decree (*alvará*) of 10 February 1750. The following year the Royal Treasury also contributed 750,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) towards building the great wall that flanks the road leading to the church of Santa Luzia (St Lucy).

before: Even at present this church is the object of a well-attended pilgrimage on 7 and 8 September each year. After the great pilgrimages of Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of the Mount), of the Milagres at Machico and of the Lord Jesus (*Senhor Jesus*) at Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), it is one of those that draw the greatest crowds of pilgrims from every part of the island, and it offers the observer one of the most interesting and picturesque sights. Frutuoso’s testimony shows that it is quite ancient and has always been remarkably well attended, and so it has remained through several centuries.

before: As Pedro Vitorino says, such tombs are very rare in our country, and this specimen in the Cathedral, the only one in Madeira, therefore deserves the greatest care in its conservation. It has been claimed, without foundation, that the Fleming João Esmeraldo, who died in 1536, and his wife were buried there. The date 1425 is carved on the lintel of the portal of the chapel of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria). It is presumably meant to mark the year in which the settlement of Madeira began, and perhaps the year this chapel was built, although one may conjecture that the stone belonged not to the original building but to a rebuilding later than the date shown. It was the first church built in Madeira, and we dealt with it in a detailed article published in the *Jornal* of 27 October 1942.

before: In the Angústias Cemetery (‘Sorrows’) there is a marble stone that was formerly in the old Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi), bearing this epitaph: ‘Here lies Lois Alvares da Costa, who founded this house in the year 1473, and his son Francisco Alvares da Costa, first *ouvidor* (judicial officer of the donatary or the Crown) and overseer of the royal treasury (*vedor da fazenda*) in these islands of Madeira’. When the church of this convent was demolished in 1865 and many of the bones it contained were moved to the Angústias Cemetery, the stone was used to cover these mortal remains, and the following words were inscribed on it: ‘Family vault of the bones exhumed from the former convent and church of São Francisco (to which the original inscription refers), transferred on 2 May 1865’.

before: The text of Gaspar Frutuoso, written in 1590, contains the following references to this parish: ‘. . . Magdalena, a thing so singular and noble for the chapel of this saint which the inhabitants built there, where much profit is gathered from sugar.’ Elsewhere in the *Saudades* we read: ‘Half a league from the town of Ponta do Sol, along the sea, lies the parish of Magdalena, of up to thirty households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’). It has a sugar mill (engenho) which belonged to one Manuel Dias, and a fine estate of good land under canes, and much fresh water. In this parish there is a chapel of Nossa Senhora dos Anjos (Our Lady of the Angels) which, though small, is a rich house, with a small altarpiece, fresh and well adorned; beside it is a cool spring beneath some boulders, among sugar-cane plantations of very handsome canes.’ (See Anjos 1-71). This locality of Anjos now belongs to the parish of Canhas and was once part of the parish of Ponta do Sol; we do not know whether it may perhaps have belonged to the parish of Madalena, as Gaspar Frutuoso states.

before: Beside the road that runs alongside the Levada de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’), almost at the point where it meets the Caminho da Torrinha (‘little tower’), stands the chapel of Our Lady of Consolation. Here, in the summer season, the novenas and the accompanying feast are celebrated with great splendour and draw large crowds. We do not know the year of its construction, but we presume that it dates from the end of the 16th century. It was small, and in 1861 it was suitably rebuilt and enlarged, being blessed in July of that year. The altar front, a fine old mosaic, belonged to the church of the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi). This chapel formed part of the parish of Monte (‘hill’) before the creation of the parish of Santa Luzia, within whose bounds it now lies.

before: The parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos is one of the oldest on this island, and its creation dates back to the beginning of the second quarter of the 15th century, around 1430. The seat of the new parish was the chapel of Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit), and it was later transferred to the church of São Sebastião (St Sebastian). Around 1720 the chapel founded by Zargo, which was then in an advanced state of ruin, was rebuilt, and in 1908 major repairs were carried out there, as well as on the small house adjoining it. Although perhaps nothing now remains of the original building, this chapel is nonetheless a small historic monument for the municipality (*concelho*) and parish of Câmara de Lobos. It recalls the name of the discoverer of Madeira, who had it built, and it was also the seat where the parish was established at the time of its creation. We do not know when the church of São Sebastião was built, nor when the seat of the parish was transferred to it. We believe, however, that we are not far from the truth in stating that both took place at the beginning of the 16th century, and that in the last quarter of the following century the church was enlarged and the bell tower built. Around the middle of the 18th century very important works were carried out on the same church by order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*), which on this occasion contributed 291,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) towards a bell of 24 *arrobas* and 620,000 *réis* for vestments.

before: It was perhaps the parish in Madeira with the greatest number of chapels. Those of São Bernardino, Espírito Santo, Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora, Jesus-Maria-José, Our Lady of Nazaré, Our Lady of Prayers, Our Lady of the Good Death, Nossa Senhora da Conceição, São Francisco, Our Lady of Pity, Nossa Senhora da Fátima and Nossa Senhora das Dores in the cemetery still exist today, while those of Our Lady of Bethlehem, São João and São Cândido, and others besides, have disappeared.
after: It was perhaps the parish in Madeira with the greatest number of chapels. Those of São Bernardino, Espírito Santo, Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora, Jesus-Maria-José, Our Lady of Nazaré, Our Lady of Prayers, Our Lady of the Good Death, Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, São Francisco, Our Lady of Pity, Nossa Senhora da Fátima and Nossa Senhora das Dores in the cemetery still exist today, while those of Our Lady of Bethlehem, São João and São Cândido, and others besides, have disappeared.

before: This parish is one of the most important fishing centres in the archipelago, with some hundreds of people engaged in the arduous work of fishing. A considerable number of them live in a small quarter commonly known as Ilhéu, in sanitary conditions that leave much to be desired. Nevertheless, it is said that during the cholera epidemic of 1856 the disease never reached Ilhéu, which led the parish priest of the time to remark that the epidemic could not contend with the lack of cleanliness and hygiene in that quarter. Worship in the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception) was maintained by the fishermen, and an old set of statutes (*compromisso*) of their confraternity contained certain clauses on the assistance to be given to its members in sickness and infirmity, amounting to a kind of mutual aid, which was highly praiseworthy.

before: This is one of the three streams that run through the city, and it takes its name from the chapel of this dedication, the chapel of Santa Luzia (St Lucy), which stood on a rise on its left bank. The land along its banks was among the first to be farmed in various ways in the earliest days of colonisation. At the end of the 17th century there were four sugar mills on its banks. Important levadas (irrigation channels) rise in the basin of this stream, the chief of them being the one called the Levada de Santa Luzia (see II-255).

before: Overlooking the sea in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniçal (‘reed bed’) rises a height known as Monte Gordo (‘fat hill’) or Piedade (‘pity’). On its summit stands out the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity), which ships approaching the coast can see from a great distance. It is said to have been founded in the 16th century by Garcia Moniz, the first administrator (administrador do concelho, government-appointed head of the municipality) of the entail (*morgado*) of Caniçal. Ownership later passed to the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of São Gil (‘St Giles’), whose manor house stood in the locality of Calçada (‘paved way’), in the parish of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’).

before: 1418 – Discovery of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’)? See Discovery of the Archipelago. 1419 – Discovery of the island of Madeira? 1430 – Creation of the parishes (*freguesias*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) and Calheta (‘small cove’). 1433 – King Duarte grants the archipelago of Madeira to Henry the Navigator. 1433 – King Duarte grants this archipelago to the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*) in spiritual matters. 1440 – Grant of the captaincy of Machico to Tristão Vaz Teixeira. 1440 – Creation of the parishes of Caniço (‘reed’) and Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’). 1445 – The navigator Alvise Cadamosto (see that entry) visits Madeira and Porto Santo. 1446 – Grant of the captaincy of Porto Santo to Bartolomeu Perestrelo. 1449 – Afonso V confirms the grant made by King Duarte to Henry the Navigator. 1450 – Creation of the parish of Machico. 1451 – Grant of the captaincy of Funchal to João Gonçalves Zarco. 1451 – Funchal is raised to the status of town (*vila*). 1454 – João Gonçalves grants some land in São Paulo for the foundation of the first hospital. 1467 – The first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*), João Gonçalves Zarco, dies in Funchal. 1477 – Creation of the Funchal Customs House. 1493 – Very important measures are adopted concerning water, timber, livestock, agricultural matters, etc. 1497 – Manuel I makes the archipelago of Madeira a crown domain (*realengo*) and returns it to the crown. 1497 – Foundation of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*). 1501 – Creation of the town of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). 1501 – The 2nd captain-donatary, João Gonçalves da Câmara, dies in Funchal. 1502 – Creation of the Vila da Calheta (‘town of Calheta’). 1505 – In the convent of St Bernardino (*São Bernardino*), in the parish of Câmara de Lobos, Friar Pedro da Guarda, known as the Holy Servant of God, dies in the odour of sanctity. 1508 – The town of Funchal is raised to the status of city. 1508 – Bishop João Lobo comes to Madeira to perform episcopal functions; he was the first prelate to visit this island and stayed here about two years. 1514 – The diocese of Funchal is created. 1515 – The *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) is raised to the status of town. 1516 – Consecration of the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) of Funchal. 1517 – The parish of São Jorge is created. 1523 – Vow made by the people and the Council of Funchal to St James, who is chosen as ‘principal patron saint’ of Madeira. 1526 – The first bishop of Funchal, Dom Diogo Pinheiro, dies on the mainland. 1530 – The third captain-donatary of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, dies at Matosinhos, near Porto. 1533 – Case of the prophets Fernão Bravo and Filipa Nunes on the island of Porto Santo. 1533 – The archbishopric of Funchal is created. 1536 – The 4th captain-donatary, João Gonçalves da Câmara, dies in Funchal. 1540 – The captain-donatary of Machico, Diogo Teixeira, dies, and the captaincy reverts to the crown. 1550 – Creation of the parish of Faial. 1551 – The archbishopric of Funchal is abolished and the archipelago of Arguin is added to the jurisdiction of this diocese. 1552 – Creation of the parish of Santana. 1553 – Creation of the parish of Seixal (‘pebble shore’). 1557 – Creation of the parishes of the Sé and Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’). 1558 – Creation of the parish of Gaula. 1560 – Creation of the parish of Água de Pena. 1561 – Creation of the parish of Caniçal (‘reed bed’). 1565 – Creation of the parishes of Monte and São Gonçalo. 1566 – Terrible sack of the city of Funchal by French corsairs. 1566 – Foundation of the Funchal Seminary. 1566 – Creation of the parish of São Pedro. 1568 – Creation of the parish of Tabua (‘bulrush’). 1569 – The distinguished Madeiran and illustrious prelate Dom Manuel de Noronha, son of the 3rd captain-donatary of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, the Magnificent, dies at Lamego. 1570 – The Jesuits establish themselves in Madeira. 1571 – Creation of the parish of Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’). 1572 – Creation of the parish of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’). 1575 – Death of the illustrious Madeiran Father Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, celebrated tutor of King Sebastian. 1577 – Creation of the parishes of Canhas and Porto da Cruz. 1579 – The parish of São Pedro is abolished; it was restored in 1587. 1579 – Creation of the parishes of São Roque and São Martinho. 1580 – Deaths of the 5th and 6th captains-donatary of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara and João Gonçalves da Câmara. 1581 – Madeira begins to be ruled by governors-general, the first being the high court judge (*desembargador*) João Leitão, as representative of the Philippine government. 1582 – The parish of Madalena do Mar (‘Magdalene by the sea’) is created. 1583 – The eminent grammarian and distinguished Madeiran Father Manuel Álvares dies at Évora. 1588 – The distinguished Madeiran Dom Sebastião de Morais, the first bishop of Japan, dies in Mozambique on his way to his bishopric. 1590 – Dr Gaspar Frutuoso writes his celebrated work ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*); he died the following year on the island of São Miguel. 1593 – The phenomenon of atmospheric incandescence known as the ‘fire from heaven’ occurs on this island; it burnt all the vegetation and even set some houses alight. 1595 – Death of the illustrious Madeiran and eminent jurist Dr António da Gama Pereira. 1608 – The diocesan bishop Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos dies in Funchal and is buried in the Cathedral. 1624 – Death of the governor and captain-general of Madeira Dom Francisco Henriques, who was buried in the church of the Colégio. 1626 – Death of the governor and captain-general of this archipelago, Fernão de Saldanha. 1641 – The restoration of Portugal is proclaimed in Madeira with the acclamation (*aclamação*, formal public proclamation of a new king) of John IV. 1650 – Foundation of the convent of the Incarnação by Canon Henrique Calaça de Viveiros. 1654 – Madeira begins to be represented in the old general Cortes (Portuguese parliament). 1655 – The Retreat of the Good Jesus (*Recolhimento do Bom Jesus*) is founded by the archdeacon Simão Gonçalves Cidrão. 1656 – John IV grants the archipelago of Madeira to his daughter, Queen Catherine. 1665 – Death of Manuel Tomás, author of the poem ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*). 1668 – Great popular sedition in Funchal, which deposed the governor and captain-general Francisco de Mascarenhas and committed other acts of violence. 1674 – The diocesan bishop Dom Gabriel de Almeida dies in Funchal and is buried in the Cathedral. 1676 – The parishes of Arco de São Jorge, Camacha, Santa Luzia, Serra de Água and Paul do Mar are created. 1681 – The illustrious Madeiran João Fernandes Vieira, the restorer of Pernambuco, dies and is buried in the city of Olinda, in Brazil. 1682 – The diocesan prelate Dom António Teles da Silva dies in this city and is buried in the Cathedral. 1690 – Two corsair ships sack the island of Porto Santo and burn the church and other buildings. 1691 – Death of the distinguished Madeiran Canon António Veloso de Lira. 1699 – Great fire in the fortress of São Lourenço, destroying the residences of the governors and captains-general of the archipelago. 1704 – The governor and captain-general of the archipelago, João da Costa de Ataíde e Azevedo, dies in Funchal. 1708 – The island of Porto Santo is sacked by French pirates. 1724 – A great flash flood (*aluvião*) causes considerable damage. 1729 – Death of the distinguished Madeiran poet Troilo de Vasconcelos da Cunha. 1730 – Death of the Madeiran writer and distinguished genealogist Henrique Henriques de Noronha. 1733 – The curacies (*curatos*) of Boaventura, Ribeira da Janela and Prazeres are created. 1734 – The curacy of Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’) is created. 1743 – The town of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’) is created. 1748 – A violent earthquake causes considerable damage and some casualties. 1753 – The diocesan bishop Dom João do Nascimento dies in Funchal. 1755 – Dr Julião Fernandes da Silva writes the curious and interesting book entitled *Carta critica sobre o methodo curativo dos medicos funchalenses*. 1756 – The construction of a harbour of refuge in Funchal is decreed. 1760 – The Jesuits are expelled from Madeira. 1765 – A great flash flood causes enormous damage. 1767 – Judicial reform that definitively establishes in Madeira a *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) and a *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district). 1770 – Celebrated royal decree (*alvará*) adopting important measures concerning the island of Porto Santo, which became known as the Law of Fifths and Eighths (*lei dos Quintos e Oitavos*). 1772 – Several primary schools, three Latin classes, one philosophy class and one rhetoric class are created in Madeira. 1775 – The Treasury Board (*Junta da Fazenda*) of this archipelago is created. 1777 – The illustrious governor of Madeira João António de Sá Pereira leaves this island, summoned by the government in Lisbon to answer the accusations made against him. 1784 – The diocesan bishop Dom Gaspar Afonso da Costa Brandão dies in this city. 1786 – Heavy rain and a violent gale cause much damage. 1787 – The Jesuit college and church are handed over to the diocesan bishop to house the Seminary. 1790 – The parish of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’) is created. 1792 – Serious events arising from the persecution of members of the Masonic lodges by the governor and the diocesan bishop. 1798 – The postal service is definitively established in Madeira. 1798 – The illustrious governor and captain-general of this archipelago, Dom Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho, dies in Funchal. 1801 – Madeira is occupied by British troops. 1803 – A great flash flood causes the greatest damage and kills several hundred people. 1806 – The Madeiran poet Francisco Álvares de Nóbrega, known by the sobriquet of ‘Camões Pequeno’ (the Little Camões), dies in Lisbon. 1807 – Brigadier Reinaldo Oudinot, who directed the channelling of the streams of Funchal and the building of their walls after the great flash flood of 1803, dies in Funchal. 1807 – British troops occupy Madeira for the second time. 1810 – The diocesan bishop Dom Luís Rodrigues de Vilares dies in Funchal. 1810 – The Board for the Improvement of Agriculture of Madeira and Porto Santo (*Junta de Melhoramentos da agricultura*) is created. 1814 – The governor and captain-general of Madeira, Luís Beltrão de Gouveia e Almeida, dies in Funchal. 1815 – Napoleon passes by Madeira. 1815 – A great flash flood causes great damage. 1821 – The Constitution is proclaimed in Madeira. 1821 – *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’), the first newspaper published in Madeira, appears. 1822 – The foundation stone of a monument to commemorate the proclamation of the Constitution in Madeira is laid with great ceremony. 1823 – A special judicial commission (*alçada*) of six judges comes to this island to try and punish those who had shown themselves hostile to absolute government. 1828 – Two high court judges come to conduct a rigorous judicial inquiry (*devassa*) into political events; more than two hundred individuals are indicted, most of whom are sentenced to various penalties, chiefly exile to the overseas provinces. 1828 – The Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) squadron bombards the town of Machico and troops are landed there; they take the road to the city, which they occupy, and absolute government is then proclaimed. 1829 – The distinguished Madeiran Dr João Francisco de Oliveira dies in Lisbon. 1832 – Constitutional troops from the Azores, commanded by Luís Mousinho, occupy the island of Porto Santo. 1832 – The illustrious Madeiran and distinguished writer Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar dies in Lisbon. 1835 – Construction work begins on the levadas (irrigation channels) of Rabaçal. 1836 – The lyceum (state secondary school) of Funchal is created; it opened the following year. 1836 – The Funchal Commercial Association (*Associação Comercial do Funchal*) is founded. 1837 – The Funchal Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-Cirúrgica*) is created and opened. 1838 – The library of the Municipal Council of Funchal is installed and opened to the public. 1838 – The Angústias cemetery is solemnly blessed and inaugurated. 1840 – The São Pedro market is completed and opened to the public. 1840 – The great poet António Feliciano de Castilho arrives in Madeira. 1842 – Great storms and a flash flood cause much damage. 1846 – José Silvestre Ribeiro is appointed civil governor of this district. 1846 – Governor José Silvestre Ribeiro introduces the great service of public street lighting in Funchal. 1846 – The famous Protestant propagandist Dr Robert Kalley is violently forced to leave Madeira, amid various disturbances. 1847 – Queen Adelaide of England comes to Madeira and stays several months. 1847 – The governing board (junta governativa) is installed, as the events begun in the country by the Junta of Porto have their repercussions in Madeira. 1847 – Known as the ‘year of hunger’, because of the dreadful food crisis this archipelago suffered. 1847 – The Funchal asylum is created on the initiative of José Silvestre Ribeiro, and still bears his name today. 1848 – The parishes of Ribeira da Janela, Achadas da Cruz and São Roque do Faial, previously autonomous curacies, are created, and in the same year the parish of Quinta Grande (‘large estate’) is created. 1848 – Construction of the bridge over the Ribeiro Seco and start of work on the road leading from there to Câmara de Lobos. 1849 – The construction of the Lazareto (‘quarantine hospital’) at the mouth of the Ribeira de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires’s stream’) is decreed. 1850 – A boat from Porto Santo is wrecked on that island’s beach, and fifteen people die. 1850 – On the initiative of the civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro, a natural history museum is established in the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace). 1852 – A vine disease known as *mangra* (powdery mildew of the vine, oidium) begins to spread and cause the greatest damage, giving rise to one of the worst crises Madeira has ever endured. 1853 – Princess Maria Amélia, daughter of Pedro IV, dies in Funchal. 1853 – In memory of her daughter, Empress Amélie founds the Hospício da Princesa D. Maria Amélia, which was provisionally housed in a building in Rua do Castanheiro; in 1862 it moved permanently into the magnificent building the Empress had built for the purpose and endowed with the funds needed for its regular running. 1856 – Madeira is ravaged by one of the greatest calamities ever to afflict it, the epidemic of cholera morbus, which kills about ten thousand of its inhabitants. 1856 – In May of this year more than twenty schools for both sexes are created in various parishes of this archipelago. 1857 – The illustrious Madeiran Dr Lourenço José Moniz dies in Lisbon. 1858 – Prince Luís, later King of Portugal, visits this island for the first time. 1860 – Empress Elisabeth of Austria visits Madeira and stays here several months. 1861 – The illustrious Madeiran Viscount Jervis de Atouguia dies in Lisbon. 1862 – The Associação de Beneficência do Funchal (Funchal Charitable Association) is founded; today it is called the Associação de Socorros Mútuos ‘4 de Setembro de 1862’. 1865 – The distinguished university professor and illustrious Madeiran Dr Justino António de Freitas dies in Coimbra. 1866 – The distinguished Madeiran and eminent teacher Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça dies in Funchal. 1868 – Serious events on the beach of this city, with dead and wounded, when the people prevented the landing of the distinguished Madeiran Jacinto de Sant’Ana e Vasconcelos, who was coming to this island to pursue his candidacy for deputy. 1869 – The illustrious novelist Júlio Dinis, author of the exquisite book *Os Fidalgos da Casa Mourisca*, arrives on this island for the first time. 1870 – Death of the eminent physician and distinguished Madeiran Dr António da Luz Pita. 1870 – Serious events in Machico at the time of the elections; some people are killed by the bullets of the armed forces, which found themselves compelled to use violence. 1872 – A great smallpox epidemic kills about a thousand people. 1873 – The Madeiran Sugar Manufacturing Company (*Companhia Fabril de Açúcar Madeirense*) is organised; it had the great São João factory built. 1873 – Publication, by the illustrious teacher and lawyer Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, of the part of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso’s celebrated work ‘Longing for the Homeland’ that deals with Madeira, which he enriched with extensive and learned annotations. 1874 – Madeira is linked to the mainland by a submarine cable. 1874 – The illustrious Madeiran Dr Nicolau Anastácio de Bettencourt dies in Angra do Heroísmo. 1875 – The judicial districts of Santa Cruz, Ponta do Sol and São Vicente are created. 1875 – The Banco Comercial da Madeira is founded in this city. 1876 – Great storms drive several ships on to the beach at Funchal. 1876 – The *Diário de Notícias*, the first daily newspaper published here in Madeira, appears. 1876 – The distinguished poet and illustrious Madeiran José António Monteiro Teixeira dies in Funchal. 1877 – Creation of the preparatory course at the Funchal Seminary and, a few years later, the installation of a regional museum of natural history specimens. 1878 – Large-scale emigration to the Sandwich Islands begins. 1879 – The circulation of foreign coin in Madeira, which had previously been legal tender, is prohibited. 1880 – The illustrious Madeiran Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, Archbishop of Goa, dies in Lisbon. 1884 – Serious events in the parish of Ribeira Brava during the election of deputies, with several people killed. 1887 – Serious disturbances of public order in many parishes of Madeira, aimed at preventing the installation of the Parish Councils; this popular movement had very grievous consequences and became known among the people as the *Parreca* (popular name for the 1887 parish councils and the riots against them). 1888 – Inauguration of the Funchal Volunteer Fire Brigade. 1888 – The ‘Manuel de Arriaga’ theatre, originally named D. before: Besides the church of the College of São João Evangelista (St John the Evangelist) (*Colégio de São João Evangelista*), the Jesuits owned the residences of Pico dos Frias (‘the Frias’ peak’), near the Pico (‘peak’) fortress (*Fortaleza do Pico*), of Pico do Cardo (‘thistle peak’), in Santo António (‘St Anthony’), of Nossa Senhora do Socorro (Our Lady of Succour), in Caniço (‘reed’), and of Fundoa, in São Roque, on the right bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’). before: The upkeep of the community, the religious solemnities and other acts of worship, the pious obligations imposed by the benefactors and donors of the college and church, and the other obligations inherent in the religious orders all called for great expense. This was met from the substantial revenues the Jesuits held on this island. If we give full credence to the documents published on p. 747 and following of the *Saudades*, we see that the Society of Jesus had an income in Madeira of 10,808,049 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). before: Penitential processions were held either to beg heaven for rain or some other favour, or to show the population’s sorrow for some offence committed against Providence. Some fifty-odd years ago the image of Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of the Mount) was taken out in procession along the Caminho dos Saltos (‘falls’), across the Levada (‘irrigation channel’) and back to its church by the Caminho do Monte. Along this whole long route the image was accompanied by numerous penitents who either carried heavy loads or scourged themselves or wounded themselves with brambles (1921).

before: ). As already stated in the article Acciaily, Simão Acciaioly was the first to come to Madeira bearing this surname. He belonged to one of the most distinguished families of Florence and was the son of Zenóbio Acciaioly and Dona Catarina Delfina. He arrived on this island in the first quarter of the 15th century, and in 1529 he was granted a coat of arms and confirmation of his nobility. Noronha says that Simão Acciaioly married Dona Maria Pimentel and that he died on 15 February 1544. He founded the entail (*morgado*) known as that of Nossa Senhora do Faial or da Natividade, and his son Zenóbio Acciaioly succeeded him in the administration of the entailed estate (*vínculo*). Simão Acciaioly owned sugar mills and a large house in Funchal, and here he held the post of *almoxarife* (royal revenue officer and storekeeper). He had the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity) built in the old chapter house of the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi), and he was buried there.

before: In 1560 the city of Funchal was sacked by French Lutheran corsairs, of whom the old Madeiran chronicles speak with such horror. The nuns of St Clare were forced to abandon their convent so as not to fall victim to that horde of savages and, as Frutuoso says, ‘they went out through the cane fields and took refuge, and did not stop until they reached their Curral, which lies a good distance from the city, and so they departed without saving any ornament, leaving everything in the convent except the monstrance of the Most Blessed Sacrament...’. The French remained in Funchal, busy with destruction and slaughter, from 3 to 17 October. Soon after they left the island, the nuns left the Curral and returned to their convent in the city. We do not know whether the nuns of St Clare had by then already built in the Curral the chapel of Santo António (St Anthony of Padua), which stood there until the middle of the 19th century and belonged to the same convent.

before: Before it was raised to a parish (*freguesia*), Curral das Freiras belonged to the parish of Santo António, from which it was separated in 1790. The Curral nevertheless had its own chaplains, who lived there more or less permanently; in 1678 a chaplain’s licence was issued to Father Cristóvão Vieira. Services were held in the chapel of Santo António. When it was inspected in 1756 by the episcopal visitor (*visitador*, ecclesiastical inspector) Dr António Mendes de Almeida, he ordered, in a visitation decree (*provimento*) recorded in the archive of the parish of Santo António, that the abbess of the Convent of St Clare be told to supply the chapel with the objects needed for worship, as she was obliged to do, on pain (*pena*) of further proceedings.

before: The learned annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) says that the parish of Curral das Freiras had its seat in the chapel of Santa Quitéria (St Quiteria), founded by Simão de Nóbrega. This is a plain mistake, for that chapel stood in the parish of Santo António, at the locality (*sítio*) that still bears that name today. It is an established fact that the small chapel of Santo António, which stood in the Curral and belonged to the Convent of St Clare, served as the base and seat of the new parish when it was created by royal decree (alvará régio) of 17 March 1790.

before: It is the parish of Madeira that bears the strongest resemblance to our picturesque province of Minho, the so-called Garden of Portugal. One detail, deserving the highest appreciation, should be stressed here: in spring and summer the most central roads of the parish of Santana are transformed into the walks of a vast and enchanting *quinta* (country estate). They are lined with hedges of box, hydrangeas, ferns and fuchsias (*mimos*) which, mingled with a great profusion of flowers, give these roads a charm and an appeal that can be found nowhere else. It is a detail that deserves special mention, for it is unique in Madeira and is certainly not often met with elsewhere in the world...

before: The lands that make up this parish (*freguesia*) originally belonged to the parish of São Jorge, from which they were separated around the middle of the 16th century. A small chapel dedicated to Santana (St Anne) gave its name to the locality (*sítio*), to the surrounding lands and later to the whole parish. before: The annotator of the *Saudades* gives this parish as created by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 4 June 1552. What this decree first created was a chaplaincy with cure of souls (capelania-curada), not yet an autonomous parish, which did not correspond to an autonomous parish. The first chaplain held this post together with that of parish priest of São Jorge (‘St George’). Under the said decree, this curate or chaplain had been allotted 8,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year for the parish duties of São Jorge, and a *moio* of wheat and a *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine for his service in Santana. The royal decrees of 16 February 1565, 1 March 1577 and 9 June 1581, which we have found cited in the *Índice Geral* of the Treasury Superintendency (Provedoria da Fazenda), always refer to the curate chaplain (*capelão-curado*) and set his emoluments at 12,000 *réis* in cash and a *moio* of wheat, at 20,000 *réis* and at 25,000 *réis* respectively. In the royal decree of 1 December 1588 the priest who performed the parish duties there is already called *vigário-curado* (curate vicar), and he was assigned an annual stipend (*côngrua*) of thirty *alqueires* of wheat and a quarter of wine. It was perhaps from the date of this decree, or a little before, that Santana began to form a truly independent and autonomous parish.

before: A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), Funchal. It was home to the *quinta* (country estate) that shares its name, with an excellent country house and an adjoining chapel of Santana e São João (St Anne and St John the Baptist), built in 1814; the residence itself is of older construction. See asylums (*Manicómios*).

before: It is worth mentioning here that the Arquivo Histórico da Madeira (Historical Archive of Madeira) was created in July 1931. The following year it was provisionally housed in one of the rooms of the palace of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*), where the various departments of the Diocesan Seminary operate today (1940). In 1933 the Historical Archive was transferred to the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace), where it is now permanently established, answering technically and administratively to the Directorate-General of Archives and Libraries (*Direcção Geral dos Arquivos e Bibliotecas*). Several thousand codices and documents scattered among various archives and public offices have been incorporated into it, making it the richest and most valuable repository of material for the history of this archipelago. It directs the important publication *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira*, of which six volumes have already appeared; it contains valuable material and most interesting information, and has today become indispensable to researchers of Madeiran history. It is regrettable that publication has not begun of the index of the documents in the municipal archive compiled by António José de Lamedo, to which we refer above. This publication has long been desired, and as early as 1873 the illustrious commentator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ considered it absolutely essential that it be carried out without delay.

before: The street runs from the Praça dos Lavradores until it meets the southern end of Rua da Rochinha and the Travessa do Arcipreste. It is one of the oldest streets in Funchal and was once called Diogo Afonso. Its name comes from the fact that the Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal) stood in it for many years, before it moved to the building it occupies at present. Later it was also called Rua de Santo António, a name many people still use today, because a chapel with that dedication was built there; its ruins lie on the south side of the street. Next to the hospital stood the old parish church of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’).

before: An inhabited locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’). The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Nazaré (Our Lady of Nazaré) that stands there was built in the last quarter of the 17th century by Francisco de Barros Maciel. It was entirely rebuilt in 1830 by António João Barbosa de Matos e Câmara, a descendant of the founder. It is an entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela), whose first administrator was the said Francisco de Barros Maciel.

before: The revolution found its echo in Madeira in the early hours of 29 April 1847, when the troops of the garrison rose and, on the old public promenade, solemnly declared their adherence to the revolution and to the Governing Junta of Porto. At five o’clock that morning, in the courtyard of the Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal), the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), various officials, some persons of standing and a good number of ordinary people gathered, with the armed force posted a few metres away. They proclaimed the principles of the revolution, declared their adherence to the Junta of Porto and named the Governing Junta of Madeira. It was made up of Luís de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, president; Francisco Correia Heredia, vice-president; Diogo Berenguer; Luís Agostinho de Figueiroa; Dr José Júlio Rodrigues; and António Correia Heredia, secretary. As Luís de Ornelas e Vasconcelos withdrew from the Junta’s work at once, its presidency was assumed, until its dissolution, by Francisco Correia Heredia, holder of an entail (*morgado*). The civil governor of the district at the time was the meritorious Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro. Refusing to join the revolutionary movement, he immediately left office and withdrew to the Quinta do Pico de São João and later to the Quinta do Deão, placing himself under the hospitality offered to him by two British subjects living there.

before: For some time the Jesuits lived in houses adjoining the chapel of São Sebastião (St Sebastian), in the street of that name, now called Praça do Comércio (volume II, page 359). before: ‘The corresponding niche on the Epistle side is likewise dedicated to the same Lady, under the title of Succour. Its founders were Canon João de Saldanha and his brother, the beneficed cleric (*beneficiado*) Joseph de Saldanha, both most devoted to our Society and distinguished benefactors of that Royal College. On the two sides of the transept there are also two chapels facing each other. The one on the Gospel side is consecrated to Jesus Crucified and is cared for by the noble Brotherhood of the Stations of the Passion (*passos*, wayside oratories depicting scenes of Christ’s Passion) of the same Lord, which exists in that city. The second, consecrated to the Archangel St Michael, was founded by the Reverend Father Miguel Pereyra, a very great benefactor of that college. On the Epistle side, the first is that of the Apostle of the East, St Francis Xavier, which was founded and endowed by the Licentiate Bento de Mattos. The second is that of St Anthony of Padua, and its founders were Doctor António Spínola, a famous physician in that city, and his wife Dona Francisca de São Paio, whom this college also counts among its distinguished benefactors. Of the two chapels beneath the choir, Father António Franco says that at the time he was writing they still had no founders, although they were adorned at the college’s expense. However, on enquiring of some religious who had lived in that college and celebrated Mass in its church, I learned that the chapel on the Epistle side was dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Conception), and that its founder had been one António de Oliveyra, a native of this kingdom and of the town of Pombal, who had married Maria da Rocha on that island. Having no children, they founded the chapel and gave all their property to it. In one of the clauses of their joint will and grant, the said António de Oliveyra declared that, should he die before his wife, she would be bound on the day after his death to go and hear Mass for his soul in his aforesaid chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição; and he bound himself to do the same should his wife die first. He did and declared this in order to do away with the custom and abuse wrongly prevailing in that city, whereby those in mourning did not leave the house for a whole year, not even to hear Mass on feast days and holy days of obligation. Of the other chapel beneath the choir, facing this one, I am told that it is very well adorned, for the church has very sumptuous revenues; but when I wrote this I found no one who could tell me whether it had any founder or confraternity.’

before: ‘I wrote the account of this chapel according to the information given to me by Jesuits who had lived in that college; but afterwards I received the letter from Father José Lopes already mentioned, in which he tells me the following: “In a chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição, which, although adorned by António de Oliveyra Baptista, has no founder, nor has it yet been purchased or endowed, even though the said man and his wife Maria da Rocha left it their thirds [of their estates], the amount of which is not yet known, since no inventory has been made.” After this was written, Father Lopes informed me in a letter of 10 March 1751 that the said chapel is consecrated to St Quiteria and has its own confraternity of that holy Virgin and Martyr. ‘The frontispiece and main façade of this church, which is magnificent and the finest on the whole island, was adorned with four marble statues of ordinary human size, representing St Ignatius, our founder and patriarch, St Francis Xavier, St Francis Borgia and St Stanislaus. before: Once it was recognised that the Sé parish needed to be relieved of a considerable share of its households (*fogos*, literally 'hearths'), so that parish services could be better organised, the chapel of Santa Luzia (St Lucy), standing on a rise on the left bank of the stream of the same name, was chosen as the seat of the new parish, which had been created by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 28 December 1676. The General Index of the Register of the Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*) reads: ‘Decree of the Lord King Peter II, of 28 December 1676, empowering the bishop Dom Friar António da Silva Teles to create a parish in the Chapel of Santa Luzia, assigning to the vicar a stipend (*côngrua*) and a suitable territory, with part of the parish of the Sé outside the walls and part of that of Nossa Senhora do Monte, since the curates of the Sé had nearly 6,000 souls to attend to within the city’. The first vicar was Father Amaro de Atouguia, whose annual salary was set by the royal decree of 24 July 1681 at 21,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash, 1 *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine and one and a half *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat.

before: We have already dealt, in the article Levadas on page 235 of volume II, with the abundant and rich water source called the Levada de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s channel’), a levada (irrigation channel) whose important aqueduct crosses a considerable part of this parish. Alongside the levada runs an excellent road, which stretches from near the Santa Luzia stream to the northern end of the avenue of Pedro José d’Ornelas. It offers striking views over the bay, the city and its surroundings. It is one of the sections that are to make up the planned ring road of Funchal.

before: A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), lying between the town (*vila*) and the parish of Tábua. It is one of the many *fajãs* formed along the coast by the collapse of the land that towered above them. ‘Since 1804 the *Logar de Baixo*,’ says the annotator of the *Saudades*, ‘has been much larger than before, because in that year a great part of the land of the *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) that overlooks it, split open by the storms of the preceding years, fell towards the sea and there formed a broad and productive plain. The shock of the fall was such that the sea rose above its level along the whole adjacent coast, and the tremor was felt both on land and at sea at a distance of more than ten kilometres: the sea came far inland into the town of Ponta do Sol.’ Lugar de Baixo (‘lower place’) formed part of the great estate of Lombada dos Esmeraldos (see that entry). However, when, on the death of João Esmeraldo, the property was divided anew between his two sons and his widow, Águeda de Abreu, she reserved the Lugar de Baixo property for herself as an integral part of her dowry. It is possible that on her death it reverted to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Santo Espírito (‘Holy Spirit’); it is certain, at any rate, that it was incorporated into it at a date unknown to us. It was sold at public auction at about the same time as the Lombada, being bought by the English merchants A. Criorgi & C.ª. There stands the chapel of Santo António (St Anthony of Padua), with a fine house attached, which we shall discuss elsewhere in this work.

before: According to the royal decree (*alvará*) of 5 October 1863, the limits of the city were as follows: to the south, the beaches of the bay of Funchal; to the east, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), the localities of Louros, Forca and Rochinha de Cima; to the north, in the parish of Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’), the localities of Vale Formoso, Calçada da Torrinha and Ponte do Deão; and to the west, in the parish of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), the localities of Pico, São João da Ribeira, Maravilhas, Ribeiro Seco and Ponte Monumental.

before: This surname was originally spelt Favela and belongs to an old and noble family that settled on this island at the end of the 15th century. The first to bear it here was Fernão Favela, known as the Elder, who had served valiantly in Africa and had been a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*). He married Beatriz Pires in Madeira and founded the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Piornais (‘broom thickets’), centred on the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Ajuda (Our Lady of Help), which he had founded and where he was buried. He died in 1545, according to Henriques de Noronha, or in 1537, according to the date given by Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo. His son and successor was António Favila, who died in 1601 and lies buried in the Ajuda chapel. Dona Inês Moniz, who was born in 1553 and died in 1589, was the daughter of António Favila. She founded an entailed estate in favour of her niece Dona Isabel Acciaioli de Vasconcelos, with the clause that it should pass in perpetuity to the eldest daughter – an extremely curious circumstance and, we believe, a very rare one, at least here in Madeira.

before: Despite the name it keeps, the parish does not lie on the summit or slopes of an isolated mount, but halfway up the high mountains that encircle the outskirts of the city. The large nucleus of population that formed in Funchal on the shores of the ocean in the very earliest times gradually spread out across the surrounding ridges and hillocks, sometimes seeking out trackless and almost inaccessible places. It was not long before the clearing of woods and thickets, and the corresponding breaking of the land for cultivation, reached the heights of this parish, at least within the limits where it bordered on the original Funchal. The homesteads slowly advanced up the steep mountainside, and higher up there already stood the small and devout chapel of Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of the Mount), which lent its name to the locality (*sítio*) and later to the future parish.

before: This parish had its origin in the settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) that Adão Gonçalves Ferreira held there. He was the first man born on this island and the son of Gonçalo Aires Ferreira (see p. 21), the most distinguished companion of Zargo in the discovery of the archipelago. As was generally the case, a small chapel was the centre around which the first settlers gathered: around 1470 Adão Ferreira built a modest chapel there, which seems originally to have been called Nossa Senhora da Incarnação (Our Lady of the Incarnation). It later came to be called Nossa Senhora do Monte, certainly owing to the lie of the land, which fully justified the new and fitting name. Others maintain that it was the miraculous apparition of the image of the Blessed Virgin (*Santíssima Virgem*), which people at once began to call Nossa Senhora do Monte, that led the chapel to take this name, which passed to the locality and later to the whole parish.

before: The legend of this miraculous apparition is told in the following terms on the back of the engravings depicting the tiny and venerable image: ‘More than 300 years ago, at Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’), about 1 kilometre above the church of Nossa Senhora do Monte, a little Girl played one afternoon with a certain young shepherdess and gave her a snack. Full of joy, the shepherdess told her family of this, but they did not believe her, for it seemed impossible to them that a little Girl should appear in that lonely forest so far from the village. The following afternoon the same thing happened, and the shepherdess told of it again. The next day, at the hour the shepherdess had given, her father secretly went to watch the scene, and he saw on a stone a small Image of Most Holy Mary, and in front of it the innocent shepherdess, who, when her father unexpectedly appeared, declared that this Image was the little Girl she had spoken of. The shepherd, amazed, did not dare to touch the image, and reported the matter to the authorities, who had it placed in the chapel of the Incarnação, near the present church of “Nossa Senhora do Monte”, the name that has been given to that venerable Image ever since.’ This account does not differ in essentials from a manuscript description in our possession dating from the middle of the 18th century, which was itself based on an unbroken oral tradition. That description contains the following interesting detail: ‘On the following day at dawn Our Lady was found outside the Chapel, at the spring close by it, upon a stone on which some ancient characters, barely legible, may still be seen today…’ This most precious stone, says Father Joaquim Plácido Pereira, was buried at the bottom of the Ribeiro de Nossa Senhora (‘Our Lady’s brook’) when the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) had the Largo da Fonte (‘fountain square’) enlarged in 1896.

That description contains the following interesting detail: ‘On the following day at dawn Our Lady was found outside the Chapel, at the spring close by it, upon a stone on which some ancient characters, barely legible, may still be seen today…’ This most precious stone, says Father Joaquim Plácido Pereira, was buried at the bottom of the Ribeiro de Nossa Senhora (‘Our Lady’s brook’) when the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) had the Largo da Fonte (‘fountain square’) enlarged in 1896.

before: A year later the earthquake of 1 April 1748 (see Earthquakes), which caused so much damage on this island, left the new church badly damaged and in need of major and immediate repairs. Work began without delay, but it proceeded slowly, and its full and final completion took several years. The opportunity was taken to correct, as far as possible, some serious errors made in the construction begun in 1741, which made the cost of the repairs carried out there all the greater. According to a note entered in one of the books of the parish archive, the total cost of the works, including the church with its churchyard and flights of steps, the walls, the attached houses and various ornaments and church furnishings, was 200,445,500 *réis*, undoubtedly a very considerable sum for the time. To meet these heavy expenses, collections were made throughout the island. A large contribution also came from the Confraternity of the Slaves of Nossa Senhora do Monte, founded in 1750 by Bishop Dom Friar João do Nascimento. It soon spread to every parish, arousing great devotion among the faithful, and almost all its revenue was applied to this purpose.

before: Gaspar Frutuoso, who wrote the *Saudades* in 1590, makes no reference to the cult of Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of Monte), so widespread throughout the island, although he does mention a miraculous event (*Saudades*, p. 250) that occurred during the terrible sack of Funchal by the Huguenots on 3 October 1566. Devotion to Our Lady of Monte is nonetheless very old throughout the archipelago. From the second quarter of the 17th century onwards, the parish archive contains many references to this cult and accounts of extraordinary events attributed to the intercession of the Blessed Virgin through the devout image venerated there. Even so, it seems certain that it was only after the founding of the Confraternity of the Slaves of Nossa Senhora do Monte, around the middle of the 18th century, that the cult grew more intense and spread more widely through all the parishes of Madeira. It was then that pilgrimages and visits to the church began to draw larger crowds of the faithful, and these have grown steadily and considerably over the years. Today it is the most frequented pilgrimage festival on the whole island, with tens of thousands of people gathering there on 14 and 15 August each year.

before: After the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 9 October 1803 (vol. I, p. 54 ff.), the diocesan bishop, the cathedral chapter, the clergy and the faithful placed the island, and especially the city, under the protection of Nossa Senhora do Monte. This was confirmed by an Apostolic Rescript of Pius VII dated 21 July 1804, and the feast of the Patronage of Nossa Senhora do Monte was then instituted. It was celebrated on 9 October each year with a solemn procession from the Cathedral to the parish church of Santa Maria Maior (St Mary Major). The ninth of October was formerly a holy day of obligation, preceded by its own vigil with fasting.

before: As already stated, building work began in 1492 but was not declared complete until 1497. This slow progress must be attributed partly to the absence of the founder and captain-donatary. Having ordered and arranged everything for the building, and perhaps even begun it, he later left for mainland Portugal, where stays were always long, chiefly because of the difficulty of communications. The building was later enlarged several times as the number of nuns grew. Along the cloister, to satisfy the devotion of the nuns and of other people, many chapels and oratories were built, which were quite unnecessary for the community’s religious services. The original church, dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Conception) and known as Conceição de Cima, came to be dedicated to St Clare (see that entry), who was the patron of the monastery. This church also underwent considerable changes over time, being almost entirely rebuilt in the first half of the 17th century.

before: Bishop Dom Friar António Teles da Silva (1675–1682) enlarged the original palace, and the prelate Dom José de Sousa de Castelo Branco (1698–1721) incorporated into it the adjoining seminary, when the latter moved to the Rua do Mosteiro Novo (New Convent street). The earthquake felt in Madeira on the night of 31 March to 1 April 1748 caused considerable damage throughout the island to many public and private buildings, and the old bishops’ palace and the adjoining seminary were also badly ruined. The bishop of Funchal at the time was Dom João do Nascimento, who governed this diocese from 1741 to 1753. He proved an eminent prelate who marked his time on this island with various notable works, both in the performance of his episcopal duties and in serving for some years as acting governor and captain-general of this archipelago.

before: The chapel of this dedication on the Largo de São Paulo is one of the oldest on the island, and we believe it was the first to be built after that of Santa Catarina (see that entry). It was originally named after São Pedro and São Paulo (St Peter and St Paul). However, although the seat of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro was established there, it was the second name that endured through the ages and is still in use today. Above the portico one can still see the traditional keys, or papal arms, bearing witness to the chapel’s patron saint, or former dedication.

before: Services in the chapel of São Paulo were conducted by Franciscan friars until 1566, when the parish of São Pedro was created and its seat installed in this same chapel. The parish was abolished in 1579 and restored in 1586; it is not known whether the parish was installed for the second time in this chapel or in some other. In 1879 a confraternity bearing the name of the patron saint was organised there, and its statutes were approved by the highest authority of the district by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 13 March of that year.

before: The parish, as has been said, was created around 1450 and its parochial jurisdiction extended over the whole area of the captaincy. Chaplaincies with cure of souls, dependent on the mother church (*igreja matriz*), were later established in Santa Cruz, Porto Moniz, São Vicente, Ponta Delgada, São Jorge, Santana, Faial and Porto da Cruz. That of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) was soon made an independent parish, and the other chaplaincies gradually became autonomous parishes. The rapid growth of the population at the seat of the captaincy led to the creation of new ecclesiastical posts: a collegiate church with six beneficed clerics was established before 1572, and a curacy by royal decree (*alvará*) of 15 November 1576.

before: Within this parish chapels were built to the Lord of Miracles, which we have already discussed (vol. 1, p. 332), São Roque, Nossa Senhora do Rosário, Our Lady of Grace, Our Lady of Prayers, São Cristóvão, Our Lady of Protection, St Joseph, Santo António and Santana, to which we shall refer at greater length elsewhere in this work. before: Overlooking the sea at the western end of the bay stands the old chapel of São Roque (St Roch). At its foot rise the springs known by the name of the chapel’s patron saint, which issue from the cliff almost at the level of the ocean’s waterline. These waters have excellent therapeutic properties, and their use is especially recommended for certain diseases of the stomach. The statements of many patients and the testimony of physicians are irrefutable proof of their efficacy. The local Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) had the waters chemically and bacteriologically analysed, and the results confirmed the opinion already held of them. They draw a considerable number of people to this town in the hot season. For this reason, and because of its bathing beach, the place is gradually becoming a popular spa and seaside resort. Another powerful attraction is the enchanting beauty of the spot and the complete absence of heat, which together make the town of Machico one of the most sought-after places in Madeira in which to spend the summer.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), where the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of the Mount) stands. before: In the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), at the locality (*sítio*) to which it gave its name, Diogo da Costa de Quintal built a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora das Angústias (Our Lady of Anguish) in 1662. There stands the *quinta* (country estate) of Nossa Senhora das Angústias, better known as the Quinta Lambert, which has a chapel of this dedication, perhaps a rebuilding of the old chapel that existed at that locality. Princess Maria Amélia lived at this *quinta* and died there on 4 February 1853.

before: Another chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Piedade once stood in the locality called Vargem de Baixo (‘lower meadow’), in the parish of Calheta (‘small cove’). It was built in 1657 by Captain António Moniz de Meneses and his wife, Dona Catarina de Meneses. Within the lands of the entailed estate of Vale da Bica (‘spout valley’), on the Lombada dos Esmeraldos (see that entry), in the parish of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), at the place called Jangão, a small chapel with the same dedication was built in a year we cannot establish. In 1777 the administrator of that entailed estate (*vínculo*), Francisco de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, enlarged and improved the chapel, and on 3 August of that year permission was granted for it to be blessed anew. On 12 October 1879 the Archbishop of Goa, Dom Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, blessed the chapel again and celebrated Mass in it, after the repairs carried out at the orders of his brother, the peer of the realm Agostinho de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, 15th administrator of the said entailed estate of Vale da Bica.

before: On the *quinta* (country estate) of Cruzes, with its door opening onto the square of the same name, stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade, founded by Francisco Esmeraldo Henriques, who owned the *quinta*. The date 1692 is carved on the portico, but the deed of endowment is dated 25 May 1695, and on 14 June of that year the chapel was inspected so that divine services could be celebrated there. It at present (1921) contains a burial vault said to hold the mortal remains of Urbano Lomelino (see Lomelino), founder of the convent of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (see that entry) in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz.

before: In the locality (*sítio*) of Paço (‘manor house’), in the parish of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), Father Manuel de Andrade had a chapel consecrated to Nossa Senhora da Piedade built in 1784; its deed of endowment is dated 16 December of the same year. In the parish of Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’) there is also a chapel with the same dedication, founded in 1736 by João de Couto Cardoso, holder of the entail (*morgado*), next to the houses where he lived. One of his successors, Francisco João de Vasconcelos Couto Cardoso, had it rebuilt in 1825 because of its advanced state of ruin, enlarging it and moving it to the vicinity of the old chapel. It has served as the parish church. Its present owner (1921) is Francisco João de Vasconcelos, a direct descendant of its founder and restorer.

before: We do not know whether the name goes back to the earliest days of colonisation. We do know, however, that in the third or last quarter of the 16th century a small chapel was built there with the dedication of Vera Cruz (True Cross). It is possible that the common people’s tendency to simplify language shortened the longer expression Vera Cruz to the single syllable Cruz, and that in this way the chapel of the Cruz gave its name to the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) or *achada* (small plateau) near which it was built. That is, unless we accept that the present name of the parish existed before the small chapel was built, which would not be easy to establish today. It was certainly in this chapel of Vera Cruz that, in the third quarter of the 16th century, a curacy (*curato*) dependent on the collegiate church of Calheta was established. It was short-lived, however, and was abolished in 1577 by Bishop Dom Jerónimo Barreto. Its abolition was due to the slow growth of the population, which at that time must have been very small and which, over the years, has still developed little. The abolition of this curacy and of three or four others in similar circumstances led to the creation and funding of a new canonry in Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*).

before: The old chapel of Vera Cruz, which stood near the locality (*sítio*) of Calvário (‘Calvary’), did not give the name of its dedication to the patron saint of the parish. before: This is the chapel of Santa Maria Madalena, which gave its name to the locality (*sítio*), more commonly known by the popular shortened form of Madalena (‘Magdalene’). After Santo Amaro (‘St Maurus’), it is the oldest chapel in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António. We lack, however, the precise information needed to determine when it was founded, which does not seem to us to be later than the first quarter of the 16th century. The earliest reference to it that we have found dates from 1593, the year in which it received the grant of a quit-rent (*foro*). After the aforementioned chapel of Santo Amaro, it was also the most important in that parish for its antiquity, its size and its architectural style, and also for the devotion the faithful showed to its patron saint. It even came to own property of its own, of some importance, for the maintenance of its worship, something we are not aware that any other chapel in this parish possessed.

before: This distinguished lady was born in Madras, in British India, on 3 October 1840. She settled in Madeira in 1880, and two years later she founded a school in the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace), which she named St. Georges High School and which was widely attended by girls from the best Funchal society. Having closed the school around 1892, she rebuilt the old hospital of the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) with money raised from alms. There she took in a number of patients and set up a pharmacy, rendering outstanding services to the sick and the poor of that municipality (*concelho*). She was the founder of a diocesan religious community which, through its hospital work and its teaching in many schools scattered across various parishes, earned the highest praise and the gratitude of the people of this island.

before: Apart from the bays of Funchal, Porto Santo and Abra, the cove of Machico is the widest and most picturesque in the archipelago. It is fringed by a fine stretch of beach and overlooked by two roads, and it opens directly onto a most beautiful valley that extends for several kilometres along the green banks of the stream. The centre of the town (*vila*) is linked to the landing quay by a handsome tree-lined road, which makes the most pleasant of walks on calm summer evenings. Many years ago a landing place was built near the southern end of the cove, beside the chapel of São Roque (St Roch), but it was later entirely abandoned. On the other side of the bay a quay was planned, making use of a reef (restinga) there, together with a road connecting it to the interior of the town; these works were carried out between 1870 and 1873. As that landing place was considered inadequate, a new and larger quay was built in 1905, and it was altered and improved in 1907. At the end of 1931 three harbour lights were placed at the three points marking the entrance to this bay, and they are giving excellent service to the many fishing boats that make for this cove at night. The harbour is fairly large but shallow, so vessels of large tonnage cannot enter it. Above the site of the quay stood an old fort, known as the Desembarcadouro (‘landing place’) fort or the Fort of São João Baptista (St John the Baptist), now dismantled. On its esplanade a hospital was improvised in 1910, during the cholera epidemic that ravaged Madeira at that time.

before: In the article devoted to the Angústias (‘sorrows’) cemetery, we stated that in 1662 Daniel da Costa Quintal founded, on land belonging to his entailed estate (*morgadio*), the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Angústias (Our Lady of Sorrows), which gave its name to the street running nearby and also to the localities around it. As we have also already noted, we cannot now say for certain whether the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Angústias that stands on the *quinta* (country estate) of the same name (Lambert) is a reconstruction of the old chapel of the same dedication, or whether Daniel da Costa Quintal’s property might have been located there. We are inclined to think so. When the Quinta das Angústias passed into the possession of Nicolau Hemiterio de la Tuelière, and later into that of the Count of Lambert, the house, the chapel and the adjoining grounds were greatly improved, and it became one of the most pleasant and comfortable residences in Funchal. Queen Adelaide of England (see that entry) lived on this *quinta* from 3 November 1847 to 11 April 1848, and the Duke of Leuchtenberg (see that entry) also lived there from 27 August 1849 to 23 April 1850. The widowed Empress of Brazil, Empress Amélie (see that entry), accompanied by her daughter Princess Maria Amélia (see that entry), took up residence there on 28 August 1852. The ill-fated princess died in this house on 4 February 1853. Three months later, on 6 May, the coffin containing the princess’s mortal remains left the chapel of the *quinta*, followed by the empress, and was taken on board at the Cais da Pontinha (‘little point’).

before: The date that the annotator of the *Saudades* gives for the creation of this parish seems to us to be inaccurate. The year 1517, which he indicates as such, can only refer to the appointment of a chaplain of its own, who was given authority to perform certain parochial functions. The creation of São Jorge as an autonomous parish must be contemporary with that of Faial, and perhaps even somewhat later, since it is certain that the latter parish was created in 1550, having had its own chaplain since 1519. The oldest document we have found cited concerning the parish of São Jorge is that of 4 June 1552, which increased the parish stipend (*côngrua*) and fixed it at one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat, one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine and 8,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash; at that time the parish priest combined service in this parish with the chaplaincy with cure of souls (capelania-curada), not yet an autonomous parish, of Santana. We have reason to believe that the parish of São Jorge was created only a little before the date of that document. The royal decree (alvará régio) of 27 November 1572 granted the parish priest an annual salary of 25,000 *réis*, the parish then having 106 households (*fogos*, literally 'hearths'), and that of 20 April 1589 added to this salary a further thirty *alqueires* of wheat and a quarter of wine.
