before: Besides the chapel already mentioned, there was once that of Nossa Senhora do Rosário (Our Lady of the Rosary), in the locality (*sítio*) of Ilha, and that of São Pedro (‘St Peter’) still exists; we shall give a brief account of both elsewhere in this volume. Compared with other parishes of Madeira, this one has no great unevenness of terrain and is extremely picturesque. It offers the visitor beautiful and surprising panoramas and, like Santana, bears a strong resemblance to the enchanting landscapes of the Minho.

before: We have already said elsewhere that João Gonçalves Zarco had his first residence on the heights of Santa Catarina, built perhaps from the rich and fragrant cedars that grew everywhere in dense woods. before: Within a few years the growing number of new settlers and their immediate descendants formed a very substantial nucleus of population, which soon made the creation of a parish advisable. The densest settlement stretched along both banks of the stream, which was the boundary between the two captaincies. On either side of this watercourse two parish churches were built: the one on the right bank had the Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit) as its patron saint, and the one on the left bank Santo Antão (St Anthony the Great). The lands around the first were called Caniço para a Cidade (‘Caniço towards the city’), and those around the second Caniço para Machico (‘Caniço towards Machico’). These names clearly indicated the captaincies to which they belonged.

before: Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo gives 1440 as the year in which this parish was created, and it is certainly one of the oldest on the island. before: It owes this name to the fact that its original parish church was larger than the chapel built by João Gonçalves Zarco on the site where the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) stands today, both being dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Conception). In former times it was also known as Conceição de Baixo (Lower Conceição), the other being called Conceição de Cima (Upper Conceição). It was likewise called Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), because it was built not far from the beach; this is the name that has lasted longest among the people, and it is still in use today. This parish became widely known, and still is at present, as the parish of Socorro (‘succour’), a name applied especially to the part of it lying between the parish church and the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’). The name came from the image of Nossa Senhora do Socorro (Our Lady of Succour), which was venerated in the parish church and was in former times the object of fervent devotion among the inhabitants of Funchal.

before: There was once in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’) a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Conceição, founded by Tristão de França Bettencourt in a year unknown to us. In 1906 a chapel with the same patron saint was built in the Largo das Babosas (‘aloes’), in the same parish. It was founded to commemorate the jubilee celebrations held in Madeira to mark the fiftieth anniversary of the definition of the dogma of the Immaculate Conception. The main part of these festivities was an imposing and brilliant religious procession that set out from the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) and made its way to the Largo da Fonte (‘spring’), in the parish of Monte, where an open-air Mass was celebrated. On that occasion the prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto delivered one of his most stirring and enthusiastic speeches. It was then that the idea arose of building the Chapel-Monument, which was carried out two years later; the diocesan bishop had first appointed a committee to raise the necessary donations and to direct the construction. Commander João Bernardino Gomes, vice-president of the committee, donated the land for the building of this graceful church and the image of the Virgin that stands on its altar, and there were other generous gifts for the ornamentation and decoration of the chapel. Justice demands that we record here that it was Commander Luís de Bettencourt Miranda who contributed most notably to the construction of the Chapel-Monument. To his diligent and persevering efforts is owed not only the completion of all the work but also the embellishment of the site, which became an exceedingly picturesque spot and an obligatory place to visit for all who go to the enchanting, paradisal resort of Monte. The pamphlet *Nossa Senhora do Monte*, by Father Joaquim Plácido Pereira, contains a detailed account of the jubilee celebrations and the founding of this chapel.

before: In the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), a short distance from the parish church, stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Conception), which is very old and is presumed to have been built by the people. Over time it has undergone various repairs, and only about twelve years ago major work was carried out there for its preservation and interior decoration. This chapel, which is not particularly small, is in the care of the fishing community, which maintains and supports worship in it.

before: In Rua da Carreira (‘track’), in this city, between Rua do Conde de Canavial and Rua da Alegria (‘joy’), stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição. It was founded in 1770 by Captain Luís Bettencourt de Albuquerque e Freitas next to his residence, and was blessed on 7 December of that year. In the parish of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), at a spot unknown to us, Rui Dias de Aguiar and his wife Leonor de Ornelas de Andrade founded in 1662 a chapel of the same dedication, whose deed of endowment was dated 11 December of the same year.

before: On the property he owned in the parish of São Roque (‘St Roch’), Canon António Lopes de Andrade founded in 1700 a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Conceição, its deed of endowment being dated 8 July of the same year. Diogo Afonso de Aguiar founded in 1688 a chapel in the parish of Tabua (‘bulrush’), likewise dedicated to Our Lady, which he had built very close to the shore. It was rebuilt in 1910 by José da Silva Novita and was blessed by the prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto on 31 July of the same year.

before: The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição in the parish of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’) was the seat of an important entailed estate (*morgadio*), which covered one of the largest properties on this island. A few years ago its last owner sold it off in plots, and the chapel and the adjoining manor house were also sold. The chapel was founded by André de França e Andrade around 1672.

before: The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição in the locality (*sítio*) of Amoreiras (‘mulberry trees’), in the parish of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), is of very recent construction. It was blessed on 27 December 1911 and was founded by the parish priest José Marcelino de Freitas with donations from the faithful.

before: Also dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Conceição are a chapel in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), founded around 1600 by Bartolomeu Telo Moniz de Meneses, and another in the parish of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), rebuilt in 1754 by Nuno de Freitas da Silva; the year of its original construction is unknown.

before: In the locality of Fajã dos Padres (‘the priests’ flat’), on the coast of the parish of Campanário (‘bell tower’), there was once a small chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Conceição, which belonged to the Jesuits and was destroyed by Algerian corsairs in 1626.

before: We do not know where the seat of the parish was established when it was created. We conjecture that a chapel of the Holy Trinity (*Santíssima Trindade*) already stood there and that the seat of the new parish (*freguesia*) was installed in it, as generally happened throughout the diocese in the early days of colonisation. It was no doubt a chapel of modest proportions, which must have undergone various repairs and perhaps enlargements until a church of more ample dimensions was built. The building that served as the parish church before the present one was destroyed by a flash flood (*aluvião*). It stood opposite the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception), and traces of the original building can still be seen on the site. An order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) dated 22 October 1675 decreed that a new church be built. However, it seems that the work either did not begin at once or proceeded very slowly, for on the façade of the church one reads the inscription ‘Rei Dom Pedro – 1696’ (King Dom Pedro), which is certainly the date of the building’s completion.

before: This parish has the chapels of Madre de Deus (Mother of God) and of Nossa Senhora da Conceição, of which we have already given a brief account on pages 312 and 432 of volume II, and that of Nossa Senhora da Candelária (Our Lady of Candelaria), about which we know no particulars whatsoever.

before: This locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Canhas takes its name from the chapel of Nossa Senhora dos Anjos (Our Lady of the Angels). The chapel is of considerable age and was built, according to some, by order of the Infanta Dona Beatriz, as guardian of her son, the Grand Master of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), to which Madeira belonged in spiritual matters; according to others, it was built by Martins Afonso in 1508. The image venerated in this chapel was the object of great devotion, and Friar Agostinho de Santa Maria discusses it in vol. X of his *Santuário Mariano*. The locality of Anjos, which is exceptionally fertile and forms the coastal strip of the parish of Canhas, was once part of the parish of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’).

before: It ran between the Largo of the College (*Colégio*) and Rua das Pretas. before: A family surname of French origin, now extinct in Madeira. Felipe Gentil de Limoges founded the entail (*morgado*) and chantry (*capela*) of São Filipe (St Philip), in Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’). See São Filipe (chapels).

before: In the locality (*sítio*) of Pico, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of the Mount), stands the *quinta* (country estate) of this name, also known as Quinta Cossart. It is one of the most sumptuous residences in Madeira, and we have already given a brief account of it on page 461 of volume II of this *Elucidário*.

before: On the spot now occupied by the locality (*sítio*) of Casais (‘hamlets’) there once stood a small chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity). The year of its foundation is unknown, but we presume that it must date from the third or last quarter of the 16th century. It had its own chaplain, who performed the religious services there under the authority of the vicar of São Jorge. It was this chapel that served as the seat of the new parish, created by the diocesan prelate Dom António Teles da Silva under the authority granted by the royal decree (alvará régio) of Peter II of 28 December 1676.

before: Long before the parish was created, the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade was already in a lamentable state of repair and threatening imminent ruin. Only ten years after the parish seat had been installed there, Bishop Dom Estêvão Brioso de Figueiredo, who visited it in person, ordered that the immediate construction of a new church be requested, because of the cramped dimensions of the small chapel, which he considered unfit to serve as the parish church. It was only half a century later, by order of the Council of the Exchequer (*Conselho de Fazenda*) of 18 January 1740, that the building of the new church was ordered. It was blessed on 19 March 1744 by the vicar of the time, Father Manuel da Costa.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’). It has a chapel dedicated to Santo António (St Anthony of Padua), built in 1705 by Inácio Viana do Rego, with an adjoining manor house that belonged to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of the Heredia family, whose last representative was the Viscount of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’).

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’). Here stands the Chapel of the Magi (*Reis Magos*), founded around 1529 by Francisco Homem de Gouveia, who made it the seat of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he established; the estate was later incorporated into the house of the donataries of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). In the same locality is the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Livramento (Our Lady of Deliverance), built by Dona Inácia Betencourt Perestrelo in 1860.

before: Within this parish stand the church of the College (*Colégio*), the church of Carmo (Carmelite church), the church of Bom Jesus (Good Jesus) and the church of the Misericórdia (*Igreja da Misericórdia*). The chapels of St Sebastian, St Bartholomew, São Lourenço, Our Lady of Pity, Jesus Maria José, Our Lady of Grace, Our Lady of Deliverance and Nossa Senhora dos Varadouros (Our Lady of the Varadouros) no longer exist; we have referred to all of them elsewhere in this work. Inside the courtyard of the customs house there still survives, though now deconsecrated, a chapel whose dedication was to St Anthony.

before: According to the *Mappa Alphabetico* of the city’s streets, approved by the civil governor on 15 December 1863, the following belong to the parish, and in most cases form its limits: the south side of the Rua do Carmo (Costa Ferreira), from the bridge to the Vale stream; the north side of the same street, between that stream and the Rua das Hortas (Alferes Veiga Pestana); the western side of the latter street, below the Rua do Bom Jesus; the Rua da Conceição (Correia Heredia); the Rua da Ponte Nova; the part of the Rua do Bom Jesus between the Rua da Conceição and the Rua da Princesa (31 de Janeiro); the eastern side of the Rua dos Ferreiros, above the Rua dos Netos; the south side of this last street as far as the Rua do Castanheiro, and its north side from the bridge to the Rua dos Ferreiros; the Rua das Pretas (Câmara Pestana), at the points where the houses numbered 64 and 43 stand, belonging respectively to Dona Maria Camacho Teixeira de Sousa and José Teodoro Clerouin (1921); the part of the Rua da Carreira (Dr Vieira) bounded to the west by the Rua de São Francisco, and the eastern side of this street; the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence); and finally the Rua do Anadia, from the pillory (*pelourinho*, stone column symbolising municipal jurisdiction) to the bridge opposite the Rua do Carmo. Some consider the whole of the Rua das Hortas as belonging to Santa Luzia, and the south side of the Rua do Bom Jesus, west of the Rua das Hortas, as belonging to the parish of the Sé. The parish of the Sé has 4,083 inhabitants (1921).

before: The chapel of Santo António (St Anthony) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana (‘St Anne’) dates from the second quarter of the 16th century. It was not built in 1730, as Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo states, but rebuilt around that time. In 1729 the people asked the ecclesiastical authority for permission to reconstruct it, stating that it had been built by the parishioners roughly two centuries earlier. Its reconstruction was completed on 13 April 1730, the day it was inspected so that it could be blessed and then opened for worship.

before: We have already said elsewhere that it was in the solitary retreat of Santa Catarina that Zargo directed the initial work of colonisation and laid the foundations of the future town, which progressed rapidly and reached a remarkable development within his lifetime. There, perhaps, he dreamed of the progress of the captaincy of which he was donatary (*donatário*) and of the aggrandisement of the house he had founded, glimpsing in the near future the honours and privileges that would be heaped upon his descendants and successors. Perhaps he had guessed that the monarch would reward him with the marks of nobility and the use of a coat of arms, already seeing his grandsons’ patents of nobility emblazoned with the coronet of count and of grandees of the Kingdom, in homage to the services rendered by their grandfather...

before: The chapel of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria), the chapel of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), the Quinta das Cruzes and above all the Convent of St Clare are modest but memorable monuments that eloquently recall the discoverer and the discovery of Madeira. These buildings deserve from the public authorities, and especially from the administrative bodies based in Funchal, the respect and veneration that are everywhere paid to objects and things closely bound up with the lives of illustrious men. They have the very grave duty of maintaining these buildings and of protecting them, as far as possible, from the ravages of time. And, as we have already said elsewhere in this book, this is a fitting occasion to make special mention of the two-handed sword (*montante*) of João Gonçalves Zargo. It was always kept in the house at Cruzes, and a constant tradition, handed down from generation to generation within the family that owned it, attributes it beyond doubt to the illustrious discoverer. It was always regarded as such, and the deep veneration paid to that relic there at all times confirms the truth of its origin still further. It is an old weapon, made to be wielded with both hands, and it is not distinguished by fine workmanship. It certainly has no intrinsic or artistic value, but it is worth a great deal for its five hundred and more years of existence and, above all, for having belonged to the great navigator who discovered this archipelago. It is perhaps the sword that Gonçalves Zargo wielded in Morocco in his charges against the Moors, winning fame as a brave and daring knight. This venerable relic is now in this city in the hands of a foreigner, who keeps it with the esteem it truly deserves. It ought, however, to be in the possession of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this city. It is the duty of this administrative body to arrange its acquisition and to keep it religiously in its archives, until it can take its rightful place in the museum of art and antiquities that must one day be founded in this city (1921).

before: Frutuoso refers to the peak of Lopo Machado, above the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Neves (Our Lady of the Snows). Dr Azevedo, however, says that the surname Machado derives from João Machado de Miranda, a native of Guimarães. He came to Madeira at the call of his uncle Bartolomeu Machado, who had no heirs by his wife, Dona Francisca Velosa, and the couple together founded an entail (*morgado*) from their property in favour of the said nephew’s descendants.

before: More commonly known as São João da Ribeira (‘St John of the stream’), this chapel stands on the right bank of the westernmost stream of Funchal. Over time the stream has been called the Santa Catarina, São Paulo, São Lázaro, Santo António and São João stream, the last being the name it bears today. Some attribute the foundation of this chapel to João Gonçalves Zarco. It is undoubtedly one of the oldest in the diocese and one of the few from the 15th century still standing, although nothing of the original building survives. The Franciscan friars who accompanied the discoverer to this island built a small monastery beside the chapel and remained there until the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) was built in what was then the town (*vila*) of Funchal. Frutuoso says that, ‘the place being deserted, and a friar there… having hanged himself, these religious set up a house further down…’.

before: This account differs from that of the annotator of the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*), who states that the Franciscans ‘lived as hermits… and eleven years after the discovery, their number having increased… they gathered in community in the hospice (*hospício*) and chapel of São João, which they began to build in 1432 with some alms and the labour of their own hands, without Zargo having founded the chapel…; in 1459 the friars left the hospice of São João and set sail for Portugal…; fifteen years later Friar Rodrigo da Arruda arrived on the island…, and he re-established the community in the same hospice of São João… Around 1476 the friars settled in São Francisco’. This information from Dean Gonçalves de Andrade, which seems to us the most accurate, was drawn from the Franciscan chronicles, and he gives it as a refutation of the assertions of Father António Cordeiro.

before: In 1700, in the locality of Serrado da Adega (‘wine-cellar field’) in the parish of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), António Correia Henriques and his wife Dona Maria da Câmara founded the chapel of São João Baptista, which they endowed by a notarial deed of 17 June of that year.

before: On the stream of Calheta (‘small cove’) stand the ruins of the chapel of São João Baptista, built on the *quinta* (country estate) of São João, seat of the entailed estate (*vínculo*) established by Captain Manuel de Figueiroa, who founded this chapel in 1651. As it had fallen into serious disrepair, Dona Guiomar Quiteria Betencourt de Atouguia, widow of João Albuquerque e Freitas, rebuilt it in 1770, and a licence for its blessing was granted on 19 August of the same year.

before: As described in earlier entries, there were four friaries of the Seraphic or Franciscan order in Madeira: São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) of Funchal, São Francisco of Calheta, Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity) of Santa Cruz, and Nossa Senhora da Porciúncula (Our Lady of the Angels of the Portiuncula) of Ribeira Brava. The same order also had three convents of nuns, all in Funchal: Convent of St Clare, Our Lady of Ransom and Nossa Senhora da Encarnação (Our Lady of the Incarnation). Of these religious houses, only the church and part of the Convent of St Clare and the church of the Encarnação survive.

before: Ilhéu Chão (Porto de Santa Maria) lies about 19 miles from the harbour of Funchal (*Porto do Funchal*), 15.5 from Caniço, 14 from Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), 14.5 from Machico and 11 from the Ponta de São Lourenço. Deserta Grande (Carga da Lapa) is approximately 22 miles from Funchal. before: At the beginning of the 19th century a ward known as the British Ward was set up in the Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal) in this city, intended chiefly for the treatment of the crews of English ships calling at our port. It did not last many years, because in 1837 the Funchal Medical-Surgical School was installed in the rooms occupied by the ward. We know nothing of the circumstances of this ward’s foundation, its upkeep and operation, the reasons for its closure, etc.

before: It seems that the idea of founding a hospital here arose shortly after the colonisation of this island began. It was the discoverer himself, João Gonçalves Zarco, who by public deed of 25 March 1454 granted some land beside the chapel of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle) for the building of the new hospital. The building, which was paid for by the people, was not constructed until 1469. The hospital operated there for roughly fifteen years and was transferred to the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) around 1484. The new foundation was built on land belonging to Álvaro Afonso, who gave it for this purpose in 1483 on condition that the hospital should have six beds for poor patients.

before: We are, however, of the opinion that the hospital should be moved to a site and a building whose sanitary conditions fully meet the modern precepts of medical science. For many decades the press has advocated this move, citing the reasons briefly set out above. The Lazareto, Marmeleiros and the former convents (*conventos*) of the Incarnação and Santa Clara were put forward as the preferred places for housing the hospital, once the necessary conversion work had been carried out. Among the proposals made, those considered best and most fully suited to the desired purpose were to build new buildings in the convent grounds of the Incarnação and Santa Clara, reusing only some of the materials of the old, ruined monasteries. The authoritative opinion of the doctors confirmed the public’s preference for the site of the convent of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi). A committee made up of Drs Nuno Silvestre Teixeira, Fortunato Pita, João Francisco de Almada, José Joaquim de Freitas and José Joaquim Mendes gave its opinion, in a long and well-argued report, that the new hospital building should be erected within the precinct of the convent of Santa Clara, and it rejected the buildings of the Lazareto and Marmeleiros as unsuitable for that purpose. (See the *Diário do Comercio* for January 1910.)

before: The account of this voyage of Cook’s refers to various interesting aspects of our customs, convents and churches, means of transport, wine trade, etc. Cook and the two scholars of the expedition were greatly struck by a chapel they visited in the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi), whose walls were literally covered with human shin bones, thigh bones and skulls. Other visitors also refer to this macabre chapel with great astonishment, but it was not a unique case, for in other convents in Europe there were likewise chapels whose walls were lined with human remains.

before: Varadouros (‘slipways’) was the name given, on the beach of Funchal, to the principal point for the embarkation and landing of passengers and goods, and to the spot set aside for hauling small boats ashore. This stretch of beach must have corresponded roughly to the space occupied by the present capstans, from the waterline up to the street that today lies above them. Nearby stood the small chapel of Nossa Senhora (Our Lady), which we believe had the Assumption of the Virgin as its patron saint (*orago*), and which took the name Varadouros from its position. After the chapels of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria), São Sebastião (St Sebastian) and São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), it was among the oldest in Funchal.

before: Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘Half a *légua* from here is a parish called Jardim, of forty households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’), with a church dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Graça (Our Lady of Grace). It also has a sugar mill (*engenho*), grain land and vineyards.’ The annotator of the *Saudades* corrects this information in the following words: ‘There is a manifest error in this account because, as the above-cited documents concerning the parishes of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’) and Jardim do Mar show, Nossa Senhora da Graça was already then the patron saint of the former, and at the time when Gaspar Frutuoso himself wrote the *Saudades* (1590) the latter had not yet been established: the author was therefore referring to the former and not to the latter, as the local circumstances he mentions confirm.’

before: The curacy was created at the end of 1734, and religious services seem to have begun at the start of the following year with the appointment of the curate Manuel do Nascimento. There was a small chapel there, which served as the seat of the curacy. It was rebuilt in 1786, for on 9 December of that year permission was granted for it to be blessed. The petition requesting this permission was made by Francisco Manuel da Silva, curate of Jardim do Mar, and it states that ‘by order of Her Majesty.... the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Rosário (Our Lady of the Rosary), to which that curacy is attached, has been built anew, for it had fallen into ruin, with only the altar left standing, and all the walls of its nave have been built anew...’

before: The women groaned and sweated under the weight of sacks of sand and loads of stone, which, like their husbands, fathers and sons, they carried up from the beach to the building site, all for the love of God! Our distinguished friend Mr Francisco João de Vasconcelos not only placed his chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity) at the disposal of the Revd parish priest for the celebration of divine services, but also gave land and large sums of money, and on a single day fed at his own expense ninety-odd men who, at his request, carried stone free of charge.

before: This parish is bounded by the parishes of Paul, Prazeres and Estreito da Calheta. It communicates with the first across a beach of large boulders, exposed to the danger of stones that crash violently down from the overhanging cliffs. The other two parishes are reached by mere apologies for roads, narrow tracks cut into sheer slopes, which in recent years have undergone major and much-needed repairs. The landing place and the path leading to Paul do Mar have also been properly repaired. All these improvements were due to the initiative and diligent efforts of Francisco João de Vasconcelos, who was a major landowner there and lived there almost all year round. The building of the new church is also largely owed to the same gentleman, as already mentioned, for he was Father Martinho Fernandes’s most powerful helper in raising it. João Francisco de Vasconcelos died in Lisbon on 13 April 1928. The patron saint of the parish church is Nossa Senhora do Rosário (Our Lady of the Rosary). The parish has an official mixed school, established in 1914.

before: The seat of the new parish (*freguesia*) was set up in the small chapel of Nossa Senhora da Ajuda (Our Lady of Help), which already stood there; we do not know the year it was built or who founded it. before: Around 1425 Constança Rodrigues de Almeida, wife of the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco, founded the chapel of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria) (see that entry), and ‘beside it, says Frutuoso, she built many houses to shelter women of good life, poor *mercieiras* (almswomen: poor women kept on alms in return for serving a chapel), to whom she left alms so that they should always take care to clean and serve that house (the chapel), as is still the custom today’. before: Around the middle of the 15th century João Gonçalves Zarco donated some land beside the chapel of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle) for the foundation of a hospital, which was built at the people’s expense around 1469. It was the second charitable institution the archipelago had. This hospital remained there only a few years before it was moved to the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) and placed in the care of the confraternity of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood), which was then founded in this city and later established itself in the towns of Machico, Santa Cruz, Calheta and Porto Santo. We shall deal more fully with the hospital, which later moved to the building it occupies today, and with the Misericórdias of Funchal and of the towns in the article Misericórdias. We have already devoted a separate article in this Elucidário to the hospital of São Lázaro, whose foundation dates from the beginning of the 16th century. The mental hospital, the Manicómio Câmara Pestana, will be dealt with elsewhere in this work.

before: The buildings along the Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) stream also suffered badly. Above the Ponte do Bom Jesus the waters cut new courses along both banks, and caused considerable damage, above all in Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’), where several dwellings and shops collapsed. The same happened in Rua dos Tanoeiros and to various buildings on the left bank of that stream which formed Rua Direita (‘straight street’); these were swept away by the violence of the current. A contemporary account of the event says: ‘Whole streets disappeared with their inhabitants, and others, flooded with water and mud, left owners and tenants reduced to extreme destitution. A large part of the parish of Santa Maria Maior, together with its church, the oldest in the city, no longer exists, along with a good many of its unfortunate inhabitants; the rest, scattered here and there, flooded and abandoned, presents to the eyes of the feeling man a spectacle of grief, ruin and dismay. The streets called Direita, Tanoeiros, Valverde, Santa Maria, Hospital Velho and others were carried into the sea with an incredible multitude of inhabitants.’

before: The construction of the new residence of the prelates, the one that can still be seen today in the former Rua do Bispo, led to the Seminary's move to the house on Rua do Mosteiro Novo (the New Convent, *Mosteiro Novo*). This had been intended for a convent of nuns (volume III, page 398), but was never put to the use for which it had been built. The earthquake of 1748 left this building so badly damaged that it had to be abandoned, and the establishment moved into another house or houses, whose location we do not know, remaining there until the year 1788.

before: It seems that this old and noble residence remained in the possession of his descendants. It is certain that a century after his death it belonged to his grandson Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, who was married to Dona Joana de Eça, chief lady of the bedchamber to Queen Catherine. In 1575 it was in the usufruct and possession of a grandson of this couple, also named Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, who by public deed of 16 September of that year sold it to his close kinsman Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara, grandson of João Gonçalves Zargo. It was this Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara who was governing the captaincy of Funchal, in the absence of his nephew João Gonçalves da Câmara, the sixth donatary (*donatário*), when in 1566 this city was attacked by French corsairs, who carried out a terrible sack here and massacred some three hundred people. Gaspar Frutuoso stated in 1590 that Gonçalves da Câmara lived near the convent of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) ‘in a great and sumptuous palace’.

before: This house passed into the possession of a daughter of Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara, named Dona Joana de Noronha, and then to her son António de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, who owned it in 1624. At the end of the 17th century it belonged to Francisco Esmeraldo Henriques, who founded there the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity). The date 1692 is still visible at the top of its doorway, but the deed of grant dates from 1695, and it was in that year that religious worship began there. In this chapel there is a marble burial vault said to hold the mortal remains of Urbano Lomelino, founder of the convent that once stood in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz and one of the founders of the Lomelino family on this island. The house at Cruzes was incorporated into the entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) of this important entailed estate (*morgadio*), probably through marriage, in a year we cannot determine. It remained in this family until our own day, and a few years ago became the property of the barons of Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’).

before: In 1878 the distinguished writer Dom António da Costa published a pamphlet entitled *Instituição de Ouro*, which he later included in his notable work *Auroras de Instrução em Portugal*. before: In 1873 the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia) of the Misericórdia resolved, in accordance with the law of 22 June 1867, to found in this city a bank of agricultural and industrial credit with the sum of its loaned capital, admitting shareholders so as to increase the bank’s capital with the proceeds of the shares. A meeting was held for this purpose in the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace) on 10 July of the same year, at which it was agreed that the shares should be of 20,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) each and that subscription should open immediately. Nevertheless, the institution never became a reality, for reasons wholly unknown to us.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). before: This parish has the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity), picturesquely set on top of a hill and leaning out over the waters of the ocean. It was built on Monte Gordo (‘fat one’), or Monte da Piedade, 4 kilometres from the parish church. This is the moment to mention the unusual procession that is held every year to this chapel. The religious procession leaves the parish church and heads for the beach, where it boards several brightly decorated boats. Closely followed by a considerable number of small sailing craft, it sails to the foot of the hill, where it lands; then comes the arduous climb up the steep slope, ending finally with entry into the small, solitary chapel.

before: As the final resting place for himself and for his successors in the government of the donatary captaincy (*donataria*), João Gonçalves Zarco had the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Conception) built. It became known as Conceição de Cima and, when the adjoining convent was founded, took the dedication to St Clare, which it still keeps today. Enlarged and later entirely rebuilt in the second half of the 17th century, nothing of the original building is likely to remain there, but within its walls it holds the venerable ashes of its founder, the first captain-donatary of Funchal. It must be regarded as our most precious and revered ‘memorable landmark’, inspiring in all the most respectful and heartfelt veneration.

before: António Aluísio Jervis de Atouguia, 1st Viscount of Atouguia, belonged to a noble Madeiran family. before: A member of the Rubiaceae from the Andes, Peru and Ecuador, introduced to Madeira in 1867 by the late botanist João Maria Moniz. Of the 20 specimens that came to the island at that time, only one survived in 1909, on a *quinta* (country estate) a little above the church of Santa Luzia (St Lucy), where it flowered every year without, however, producing fertile seeds. Some cinchona trees planted in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’) did not last long there. According to the late Richard Thomas Lowe, the places in Madeira where the cultivation of the red cinchona might perhaps be tried with success are the Ribeira da Metade and the Ribeira da Boaventura, the Lombada das Vacas in São Vicente, the Montado dos Pessegueiros on the Ribeira do Inferno, the Ribeira Funda near Seixal, etc., etc. *Cinchona calisaya*, mentioned in a work on the climate of Madeira as growing in the garden of the hospice (*hospício*) of Princess Maria Amélia, was never cultivated on our island.

before: We have already given a brief account of the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Neves, where the seat of the parish was established, on page 462 of volume II. It had its own chaplain, who performed some parochial duties, and it was later raised to the status of a curacy (*curato*) by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 7 March 1566, the curate receiving an annual salary of 12,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash and one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat. The General Index of the Register of the former Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*), which we have cited so often, mentions the following documents: a royal letter (*carta régia*) of 16 September 1574, awarding the curate 20,000 *réis* a year because the curacy had more than 100 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’); a royal decree of 9 June 1581, setting this salary at 25,000 *réis*; a royal decree of 3 February 1589, adding thirty *alqueires* of wheat and a quarter of wine to the same salary; and a royal decree of 14 December 1592, fixing the corresponding stipend (*côngrua*) at 16,000 *réis* in cash, one *moio* of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. None of these documents speaks of a parish or a vicarage; they refer instead to a beneficed curate (*beneficiado curado*), albeit one with the duties of a parish priest. ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) states that the parish was created by the royal decree of 12 March 1574, yet the decree cited above, of 16 September 1574, which is later than that one, still refers expressly to a beneficed curate. From our examination and comparison of many documents concerning the creation of various ecclesiastical posts, we can state that the decrees cited in the General Index of the Crown Revenue Office are more reliable in their dates than those cited by the illustrious annotator of Gaspar Frutuoso. What seems most probable to us is that the beneficed curate created by the decree of 7 March 1566 corresponds to the creation of the parish, and that at that time the duties belonging to certain posts were confused with one another.
after: We have already given a brief account of the chapel of Our Lady of the Snows (*Nossa Senhora das Neves*), where the seat of the parish was established, on page 462 of volume II. It had its own chaplain, who performed some parochial duties, and it was later raised to the status of a curacy (*curato*) by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 7 March 1566, the curate receiving an annual salary of 12,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash and one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat. The General Index of the Register of the former Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*), which we have cited so often, mentions the following documents: a royal letter (*carta régia*) of 16 September 1574, awarding the curate 20,000 *réis* a year because the curacy had more than 100 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’); a royal decree of 9 June 1581, setting this salary at 25,000 *réis*; a royal decree of 3 February 1589, adding thirty *alqueires* of wheat and a quarter of wine to the same salary; and a royal decree of 14 December 1592, fixing the corresponding stipend (*côngrua*) at 16,000 *réis* in cash, one *moio* of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. None of these documents speaks of a parish or a vicarage; they refer instead to a beneficed curate (*beneficiado curado*), albeit one with the duties of a parish priest. ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) states that the parish was created by the royal decree of 12 March 1574, yet the decree cited above, of 16 September 1574, which is later than that one, still refers expressly to a beneficed curate. From our examination and comparison of many documents concerning the creation of various ecclesiastical posts, we can state that the decrees cited in the General Index of the Crown Revenue Office are more reliable in their dates than those cited by the illustrious annotator of Gaspar Frutuoso. What seems most probable to us is that the beneficed curate created by the decree of 7 March 1566 corresponds to the creation of the parish, and that at that time the duties belonging to certain posts were confused with one another.

before: The chapel of Nossa Senhora das Neves (Our Lady of the Snows), the original seat of the parish, dates from the 16th century, as we have already mentioned, and is among the oldest in this diocese. It underwent various alterations over the years, but by the beginning of the 17th century it was already too small for the population of the parish. Despite repeated efforts, it was only at the end of the 17th century that an order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*), dated 15 October 1697, directed that a new church be built. Construction began at the beginning of the 18th century.

before: This parish once had the chapels of Nossa Senhora da Incarnação (Our Lady of the Incarnation) and Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity), and those of Nossa Senhora das Neves and Nossa Senhora da Boa Nova (Our Lady of the Good News) still exist. We deal with them elsewhere.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of the Mount). It contains the fine residence of the Quinta da Paz (‘estate of peace’), which has an adjoining chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora do Livramento (Our Lady of Deliverance).

before: In 1662 Diogo da Costa Quintal founded, on land belonging to his entailed estate (*morgadio*), the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Angústias (Our Lady of Sorrows), which gave its name to the street that ran close by and also to the surrounding locality (*sítio*). We cannot say today with certainty whether the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Angústias that stands on the *quinta* (country estate) of the same name (Quinta Lambert) is a reconstruction of the old chapel of the same dedication, nor whether the entailed property of Diogo da Costa Quintal perhaps lay there. We are, however, inclined to think so. It was in this locality of Angústias that the bishop of this diocese, Dom Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde, while president (provedor) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*), to which he rendered the most distinguished services, had a small cemetery built in 1818. It was intended exclusively for the burial of the bodies of those who died in the Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal), and stood on land belonging to João de Carvalhal, who had given it free of charge for this purpose. When a law prohibited burials in churches, the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) obtained from the Holy House of Mercy the transfer of the small Angústias cemetery and asked João de Carvalhal, by then a count, to sell the adjoining land so that the cemetery could be enlarged. This nobleman promptly and generously offered the municipality all the land that might be needed for the planned enlargement, and informed the Council of this in a letter dated 8 July 1836.

before: The church whose patron saint was Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Conception), commonly known as Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), and which was destroyed by the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803, was already built by 1508 on the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes, near the spot where the so-called Poço do Calhau (‘well of the pebble shore’) stands today. To the east of this church lay Rua dos Balcões (‘balconies’) and Rua de Santa Maria. The latter was probably shorter than it is now, but it had many large, well-built houses in which a number of noblemen and wealthy men lived.

before: Beyond Rua dos Mercadores, at the point where the entrance to the city now stands, there were a few houses, but the place looked very different from how it does at present. The Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence) had not yet been built, and on the ground now occupied by Praça da Constituição (‘Constitution Square’) there were plantations of sugar cane. These probably extended to somewhere near Rua da Carreira (‘track’), since the building of the Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal) was begun only after 1686.

before: Outside the city stood the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), built in 1492 near the residence of the donatary, which was probably on the *quinta* (country estate) now called Quinta das Cruzes. There were also the chapels of São Paulo and of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria), the latter with an attached hospice (*hospício*) where poor women lived. It is possible that the Hospital de São Lázaro (St Lazarus) had already been built by 1508.

before: At that time, although they looked different from today, the little streets of João Tavira, Santa Catarina, Cidrão and Hospital Velho already existed, as did the squares of Corpo Santo (‘St Elmo’) and São Paulo, besides other squares and streets whose names have not survived in local tradition.

before: It is commonly called Largo das Babosas (‘aloe square’). Its new name comes from the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception) built there in 1906, intended specifically to commemorate the fiftieth anniversary of the definition of the dogma of the Immaculate Conception, and which came to be known as the Capela-Monumento. The building of this chapel is due chiefly to Commander Luís Betencourt Miranda, secretary of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal. From this square there is a striking view over the Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’) and Curral dos Romeiros (‘pilgrims’ fold’).

before: A village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico, set within the inhabited locality of Marco (‘boundary stone’). It takes its name from the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Preces (Our Lady of Prayers), founded by Canon Agostinho de Góis e Meneses in 1750 and rebuilt by António Tiago da Silva in 1884.

before: In the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) there was a chapel, now extinct, of Our Lady of Bethlehem (*Nossa Senhora de Belém*), which stood in the locality (*sítio*) of that name. It was founded in 1649 by Gaspar Vasconcelos Henriques and his wife Dona Bernardina de Carvalho, and the deed by which they made the endowment of this chapel is dated 9 February of the same year. When it fell into ruin, it was rebuilt in 1758 by Dom Francisco Inácio Telo de Meneses, a descendant of the founders. The new chapel was built a short distance from the old one, next to the residence, with which it communicated internally. In the locality of Referta (‘refuge’), at Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), there was a chapel with the dedication of Our Lady of Bethlehem, which was later renamed Our Lady of Succour (*Nossa Senhora do Socorro*). See Nossa Senhora do Socorro (chapels).

before: The parish has the chapels of Nossa Senhora do Rosário (Our Lady of the Rosary), Nossa Senhora do Livramento (Our Lady of Deliverance) and São Vicente; that of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity) no longer exists. We have already given a brief account of them.

before: The whole length of the Levada de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s channel’) road offers lovely views, with fine buildings and several *quintas* along it. Outstanding among them is the Quinta da Palmeira, one of the most beautiful in the environs of Funchal. Its owner is the benevolent industrialist and British subject Henrique Hinton, who had the window of the famous house in which Christopher Columbus lived in Funchal set up there (see vol. 1, p. 289).

before: He worked hard for the construction of the parish church of Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of the Mount), and the building of that church is owed in large part to him, above all through the creation, in every parish of the island, of the Confraternity of the Slaves of Our Lady (*Confraria dos Escravos de Nossa Senhora*), whose revenues were applied exclusively to the building of that church. He was bishop and governor of this archipelago when, on the night of 31 March 1748, a violent earthquake was felt in Madeira. It caused few casualties but did considerable damage to most public and private buildings. He took the measures that the circumstances called for at the time, and obtained substantial funds from the government in mainland Portugal to repair the damage caused by the earthquake, chiefly to many churches, to some fortresses and to the customs house buildings.

before: Its modern name is Rua do Dr. Vieira, but ordinary people know it only by its old name. ‘It is called’, say the *Saudades*, ‘the Carreira dos Cavalos [horse run] because horses were customarily raced there’. It is one of the oldest streets in the city, and in former times many of the noblest and most distinguished families of Funchal had their residences there. At present it runs from the Largo do Colégio to the Ponte de São João. Before the demolition of the Portão de São Paulo (St Paul’s Gate), near the chapel of the same name, that point was one of the limits of this street, the other being Rua de São Francisco. Besides the general name of Carreira, it bore the names Rua da Igrejinha, Rua dos Pintos, Rua de São Paulo and Rua de Manuel da Grã, each of these names corresponding to one part of the present street. The small square still called Igrejinha today, which marks the intersection of Rua das Pretas (now Câmara Pestana) and Rua da Carreira, keeps this name because a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity), commonly known as the Igrejinha (‘little church’), once stood there. Rua da Carreira is home to the old chapel of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception) and the private cemetery of the British community.

before: ‘The parish of São Pedro, in the city of Funchal,’ says Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, ‘had its origin in the chapel of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle) (see that entry), founded by João Gonçalves Zarco, which was served by Franciscan friars and later by the curates of the Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), until it was separated from the latter and constituted a parish in its own right by the royal decree (*alvará*) of King Sebastian of 20 June 1566, with the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) as its boundary to the east and the Ribeira dos Socorridos to the west. It was abolished by the royal decree of 3 March 1579 of the Cardinal-King Henry the Navigator, its urban part being reincorporated into that of the Sé, while from its suburban part the same decree created the parishes of São Roque and São Martinho; but a few years later, by the royal decree of Philip II of 14 August 1587, it was re-established with the boundaries it still has today.’

before: The seat of this parish was established in the chapel of São Paulo, which we have already described, and there is no doubt that when the parish was restored in 1587 this same chapel served as the parish church, despite its cramped dimensions. We do not know in what year the seat of the parish moved from the chapel of São Paulo to the present parish church. Nor do we know when the new church was built. On this point the annotator of the *Saudades* gives the following information, which is the same as that supplied by the *Índice* of the Provedoria: ‘Under the decree of 15 June 1598 the fabric fund of the church received 4,000 *réis*, and by various orders of the Council of the Treasury the following sums were spent on it: in 1688, on works to the church, 900,000 *réis*; from 1737 to 1739, on the building of the new church, carried out under an award by public auction (*arrematação*), 6,742,000 *réis*; in 1742, for the casting of the bells, 217,000 *réis*; and in 1757, for repairing the damage caused by the earthquake of 1 April 1748, 3,029,730 *réis*. Also in 1742 the same Council ordered the churchyard, or paved area in front of the church, and the altarpiece of the high altar to be made, but it is not recorded how much was spent on these.’

before: In this parish stand the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), which holds the tomb of João Gonçalves Zargo, and the chapels of São João da Ribeira, São Paulo, Santa Catarina, Our Lady of the Peña de Francia (*Nossa Senhora da Penha de França*), Nossa Senhora das Angústias (see Lambert (quinta)), São Lázaro, Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*) (see Moradias de Zargo), Our Lady of Pity (see the Angústias Cemetery), Our Lady of Sorrows (*Nossa Senhora das Dores*) (see Princess Maria Amélia Hospice), Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*) and Almas (see those entries). before: We believe that the ten chairs or subjects established by the decree of 17 November 1836 were not all taught in our lyceum from its foundation, and that they were only actually taught in the years immediately following. We cannot trace the various phases through which teaching at the lyceum of this city has passed across the many reforms of secondary education, because that would demand patient research that the shortness of time and the narrow scope of this work do not allow us to undertake. As we have said, the lyceum was installed in the former *Aulas do Pátio* (‘Courtyard Classes’, the public secondary classes held in the former Jesuit college), which were outbuildings of the Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*) with access from Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’). It remained there for more than 40 years. In January 1881 it was transferred to a house in the same street, a former manor house of the Vasconcelos de Couto Cardoso entail-holders which later belonged to the Barons of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), and there it began to operate on the 11th of the same month and year. In January 1914 it moved to the former bishop's palace (*Paço Episcopal*), in the old Rua do Bispo, today Rua Gomes Freire, where it is at present (1921) housed; in 1880 it had also spent some time in outbuildings of the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace).

before: The first priests to perform ecclesiastical duties were the Franciscan friars who came in the fleet carrying the earliest settlers. They served in the various chapels that were soon founded, which would have been those of Santa Catarina, São Paulo and São Sebastião (St Sebastian), and perhaps even in rustic, improvised chapels temporarily adapted for that purpose.

before: It was around 1430 that the first parish was established in Funchal, covering a vast area. Its centre was one of the chapels mentioned above, although some reasons argue in favour of the small chapel of São Sebastião. In 1438 its seat was fixed in the church of Santa Maria, or of the ‘Conceição de Baixo’, which Prince Henry the Navigator had ordered to be built on the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes, a short distance from the beach, and which took the name of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*).

before: It is rather surprising that Robert Page, who gave so many notable proofs of the nobility of his character and of his sympathy for the Portuguese, should have lent himself – moved, perhaps, by a misguided patriotism – to posing as the discoverer of the famous ‘relics of Robert Machin’s cross’ to which Dr Azevedo refers on p. 417 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), home to the old chapel of Nossa Senhora do Loreto (Our Lady of Loreto). It is the focus of a well-attended pilgrimage, drawing many people from several distant parishes and above all from the surrounding parishes. Although small, the chapel has a certain architectural distinction, and it is a pity that an ill-suited porch should spoil the harmony of the whole. It dates from the first years of the 16th century and was founded by Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, grandson of João Gonçalves Zarco, the first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal. A large manor house once adjoined it, for the founder made this the seat of the important entailed estate (*morgadio*) that he established. Others attribute the founding of the chapel and the entailed estate to Dona Joana de Eça, widow of the said Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, chief lady of the bedchamber to Queen Catherine and patron of the Convento da Esperança (Convent of Our Lady of Hope), Lisbon, where she was buried. The nuns of this convent owned a great deal of land in the parish of Arco da Calheta, bequeathed to them by Dona Joana de Eça. In the first quarter of the 20th century the tomb of the patron, Dona Joana de Eça, was found in the ruins of the church of the Convento da Esperança.

before: On leaving the embassy in Paris, Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) João Francisco de Oliveira withdrew to Funchal with his wife and children. There he devoted himself entirely to study, to the management of his household and to directing the affairs of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) of this city. He was its president (provedor) for some years and rendered it very notable services, and his portrait still hangs today in the meeting room of the Managing Board (*Mesa Gerente*) of that charitable institution. It was at this time that Councillor Oliveira founded a public class (*aula*) in surgery attached to the Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal), which he himself undertook to teach without payment. He then proposed to the central Government a plan for establishing a medical school, which received official approval but was never fully carried out. Shortly before his death he again took up residence in Lisbon, and he died there on 26 December 1829.

before: An old chronicle of this Order states that it was the Order which spiritually discovered this archipelago, because some of its members, who accompanied the discoverers, began to perform religious duties on the very day of the first landing at Machico. There they set up an improvised altar and celebrated the holy sacrifice of the Mass, which is said to have taken place on the feast of the Visitation of Our Lady to St Elizabeth of Portugal, which the Catholic Church celebrates on the second of July. There is no reason to dispute this statement, since it is certain that in the earliest days of the settlement and colonisation of this island it was the Franciscan friars who exercised all the functions of their ministry here. In the chapels of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria), São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), São Sebastião (St Sebastian) and Conceição de Cima (Upper Conception) they carried out all the parochial religious services, certainly until the time when the priests sent by the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), to which the archipelago belonged in spiritual matters, took charge of those same services.

before: We mentioned above that, according to tradition, the site for the parish church was chosen because it placed the church in a better position to escape the raids of corsairs, which is not hard to believe. The Moors of the Moroccan coast at times attacked the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and some settlements on the Madeiran coast. It may be presumed that Porto Moniz did not escape the corsairs’ plunder, since it was one of the places in Madeira closest to their point of departure, although we have no reliable record of these raids by Moroccan pirates. We have read somewhere (1921) that at the top of the town, in the place called Pedra Mole (‘soft stone’), one can still see today the remains of caves dug into the clay, where the wealthier inhabitants are said to have hidden their church furnishings and valuables whenever the corsairs approached the coast. To prevent these incursions and drive off the raiding ships, a fort was built in this parish; according to the annotator of the *Saudades*, it was the best on the north coast. It was Captain Manuel Rodrigues Ferreira Ferro, already referred to, who paid all the costs of building this fort, the State contributing only the guns and the rest of its artillery equipment. It bore the name of São João Baptista (St John the Baptist), and we are told that the stone tablet bearing the inscription recording the date and the founder of this small fort is kept in one of the military offices housed in the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace).

before: We do not know the date of foundation of the old chapel of São Bento (St Benedict of Nursia), which was the seat of the parish and of the collegiate church, though its existence must go back to the second quarter of the 15th century. This chapel underwent various alterations and repairs until the present parish church was built, which is unquestionably one of the oldest rural churches in this diocese. It has undergone various additions and modifications, but its original construction cannot be later than the second half of the 16th century.

before: Referring to this chapel, Frutuoso says: ‘... there is a church of Nossa Senhora das Neves (Our Lady of the Snows), within sight of Funchal, on a headland called Garajau (‘tern’), one *légua* before reaching the city.’ It is very old and one of the few 16th-century chapels still standing, although it has undergone some alterations over time. It was founded by João Afonso Mealheiro and his wife Catarina de Sá. Speaking of him, Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo says: ‘... he was one of the first settlers of the island of Madeira, and held a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) at Ribeira Seca, in São Gonçalo (‘St Gonçalo’), as far as Caniço (‘reed’). His wife Catarina de Sá, or Pires, founded the entail of Neves and left it to her nephew, the *almoxarife* João Cabral; but on behalf of the Royal Treasury the entail was sold to pay off a deficit in his accounts; it was bought by Lopo Machado de Góis, and his son Bartolomeu Machado founded it anew.’

before: Dr Gaspar Frutuoso is not correct when he states that the church of Calhau was the first to be built in Funchal. According to the annotator of the *Saudades*, the chapel of São Sebastião (St Sebastian) was the first to be erected here, while others maintain that the right of priority belongs to the chapel of Santa Catarina (see that entry), built of wood beside the residence of João Gonçalves Zarco. before: Porto Santo forms a single municipality (*concelho*) with only one parish (*freguesia*), that of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity), and today belongs to the judicial district (*comarca*) of Funchal. before: Each of the pilgrimage festivals held in Madeira, says the Revd Father Eduardo C. Nunes Pereira, ‘is distinguished by a special attraction for pilgrims, drawn from its general religious motive, its topography or its particular secular character. At Ponta Delgada, Monte and Arco da Calheta it is the vows; at Machico and Santa Cruz the processions on the eve, with burning candles; at Caniço, rosaries of dried pears; at Ribeira Brava, the *império* of offerings and the fisherman’s little boat; at Caniçal, the procession of boats; at Camacha, São Vicente, Porto Moniz and Curral, the freedom of the countryside and the rustic character of the place’. Every parish has its religious festivities, those of the patron saint and of the Blessed Sacrament being especially splendid, but the ones that give rise to well-attended pilgrimage festivals are the following: Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*), on 15 August; the Lord Jesus (*Senhor Jesus*) of Ponta Delgada, on the first Sunday of September; Senhora do Loreto (Our Lady of Loreto), on 8 September; the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*), at Machico, on 8 and 9 October; Piedade (Our Lady of Pity), at Caniçal, on the third Sunday of September; Nossa Senhora do Faial, on 8 September; Nossa Senhora do Livramento (Our Lady of Deliverance), at Caniço, on the second Sunday of September; Nossa Senhora do Livramento, at Curral, on the last Sunday of August; Our Lady of Remedies (*Nossa Senhora dos Remédios*), at Quinta Grande, on the second Sunday of September; that of Camacha, on the first octave day of Espírito Santo (the Holy Spirit, i.e. Pentecost); Santa Maria Madalena (St Mary Magdalene), at Porto Moniz, on 22 July; St Peter, at Ribeira Brava, on 29 June; St John, in Funchal, on 24 June; St Maurus, at Santa Cruz, on 15 January; and that of Santo António da Serra, on 13 June.

before: A German botanist, born in Erlangen in 1794, who died in Munich in 1868. Having taken part in the scientific expedition organised in 1817 by the Austrian and Bavarian governments to explore Brazil, he visited Madeira towards the end of the first quarter of the 19th century, and in his works mentions various plant species found both in Funchal and at Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of the Mount).
after: A German botanist, born in Erlangen in 1794, who died in Munich in 1868. before: Almost beside the road that leads from the Ponte Monumental (‘monumental bridge’) to the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Ajuda (Our Lady of Help). It was built by Fernão Favila on the estate he owned in São Martinho (‘St Martin’), and he made it the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*). This Fernão Favila was a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*) and fought valiantly in Africa, afterwards settling on this island, where he married Beatriz Pires. Other genealogists, however, state that it was António Favila, son of Fernão Favila, who founded the entail (*morgado*) of the Piornais (‘broom thickets’), with its seat in the chapel of Ajuda, where he lies buried, having died in October 1545. Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Manuel José Vieira, as owner of this chapel, carried out major restorations there in 1876, and it was blessed on 16 August of that year.

before: The Pontinha islet, the one nearer the shore, was joined to the facing coast between 1757 and 1762 by solid walls, as already mentioned. It is conjectured that this work was carried out when the small Fort of São José (St Joseph), which once stood there, was built, or a little before. This link, together with the stairway cut at that time into the living rock, already formed a small landing quay, which was much used when the state of the sea did not allow landing on the beach.

before: Roughly parallel to Rua de Santa Maria, and a short distance from it, runs Rua Nova de Santa Maria (‘new street of St Mary’), which was opened shortly after the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803; until then there was only a small alley there. Between the entrances of these two streets stood the church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), or of Santa Maria, which gave its name to both streets. It runs from the bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes to the Largo das Bicas or Torneiras, where Rua Bela de São Tiago begins. Today it bears the name of Latino Coelho.

before: The Franciscan friars who accompanied João Gonçalves Zarco when he began the settlement and colonisation of Funchal were the first priests to perform ecclesiastical and parochial duties on this island, in the chapels of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria), São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), Conceição de Cima, São Sebastião (St Sebastian), São João, etc. The first parish (*freguesia*) to be created was undoubtedly in Funchal, but it is difficult today to determine precisely where its first seat was. It is probable that the seat was not always the same, and even that parish duties were performed in more than one chapel at the same time. The annotator of the *Saudades* says that the first parish was perhaps established in the chapel of São Sebastião, but this is no more than a simple conjecture. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo asserts that the first church built in Funchal was that of São Sebastião, which seems to us not to be true, as we shall see elsewhere, and from this he deduces that the first parish was probably created in that chapel. The discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco first set up his residence on the height of Santa Catarina and later at São Paulo. It is certain, however, that the first and most important nucleus of population grew up not far from the beach, along the left bank of the stream that later came to be called Ribeira de João Gomes. It is therefore more likely that the seat of the first parish was established there, at least once the parish took on a more permanent character and a more definite organisation.

before: Infante Dom Luís, later King of Portugal, first visited Madeira in 1858. He was the first member of the Portuguese royal family to visit the island. Commanding the corvette *Bartolomeu Dias*, he reached our harbour on 8 October of that year, accompanied by his chamberlain, the Count of Linhares. The gunboat *Sagres* sailed in company. He landed at the Cais da Pontinha (‘little point’) the following day, and the reception was of the greatest splendour and grandeur. During the twenty days that Dom Luís spent in Madeira, besides the other festivities and public demonstrations of esteem and affection held in his honour, splendid private festivities took place, whose memory lived on in local tradition for many years because of their brilliance and extraordinary pomp. Outstanding among them were the festivity at Palheiro Ferreiro (‘blacksmith’s barn’) and the dinner and ball at the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace), given by the Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), which greatly impressed the prince; the ball at the Funchal Club (*Club Funchalense*), given by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*); and the reception at the house of the holder of the entail (*morgado*) of Cruzes, Nuno de Freitas Lomelino. Dom Luís made lengthy visits to the Asylum for the Destitute (*Asilo de Mendicidade*), the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice (*Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia*), the Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal), the military hospital, the lyceum (state secondary school) and several public offices.

before: This family surname derives from Vasco Martins Moniz de Meneses, nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*), who held a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in Caniço (‘reed’) and a large house in the town (*vila*) of Machico, and who founded an entail (*morgado*) from his disposable third (*terça*) of the estate by a will approved in 1498; and from António Telo de Meneses, or António Teles, founder of the chapel of Santo António (St Anthony of Padua) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’). The Teles de Meneses descend through illegitimacy from the Counts of Vila Pouca, according to the late Madeiran genealogist José Bettencourt da Câmara.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). It was the seat of the former entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Vale da Bica (‘spout valley’), founded in 1522 by João Esmeraldo, whose last representative was the distinguished Madeiran Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas. Here stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity), which belonged to this entailed house (*casa vinculada*). It was founded by António de Carvalhal Esmeraldo around 1670 and restored in 1777 and in 1879 by the respective administrators, Francisco de Ornelas de Vasconcelos and Councillor Agostinho de Ornelas de Vasconcelos.

before: The land that makes up this parish today originally belonged to the parish of the Sé, Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), which then extended its vast area as far as the foothills of the mountains encircling Curral das Freiras, which was separated from Santo António only in 1790.

before: It was in a chapel dedicated to Santo António (St Anthony), which no doubt originally formed part of a settled estate (*fazenda povoada*), that the seat of this parish, or at least of an autonomous curacy (*curato*), was established around the middle of the 16th century, as stated above. It is possible that before the parish (*freguesia*) was created this chapel had its own chaplain, as generally happened in similar circumstances. The chapel gave its name to the locality (*sítio*) and later to the parish; the year of its construction is unknown.

before: Over the years it underwent some alterations and even additions. However, as it had become too small for the population, which was growing considerably, a church of larger proportions had to be built. The site chosen was the ground between the present parish house and the public road, which formed part of the glebe (*passal*) and was given for this purpose by the parish priest of the time, Father António Afonso de Faria; its construction dates from the first quarter of the 17th century. Between 1665 and 1682 the chancel was added and the chapels of the Santíssimo Sacramento (Most Holy Sacrament) and of the Almas (Holy Souls) were built, and other important improvements were also made. It was not a church of cramped dimensions, for it had 6 altars and its interior was finely decorated with gilt carved woodwork (*talha dourada*). A visitation decree (*provimento*) of 1756 calls it a ‘rich church’ as regards its decoration, but by then the ‘six altars were old and ill-proportioned’, in the words of the same decree.

before: We suppose that at the end of the 17th century or the beginning of the 18th important works of rebuilding or enlargement were carried out on the old church, for in the General Index of the register of the former Royal Treasury Office (*Provedoria da Real Fazenda*) on this island we find a reference to the royal decree (alvará régio) of 9 September 1711, which ordered the continuation of the works on the church of Santo António, estimated at 2,233,920 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). We have no evidence to state that the works were completed in accordance with that estimate, but it is certain that major repairs were made to the old parish church at various times. With the building of the present church, demolition of the old one began in 1785, leaving standing the chapel of the Blessed Sacrament (*Santíssimo Sacramento*), which served as the parish seat until 1789. Next to the parish priest’s residence there still survives a stretch of wall which tradition says belonged to the old church.

before: In the early days of colonisation, and long afterwards, a good many chapels were built in various localities of this island. They generally gave their names to these places, which were often important centres of population and became the origin of future parishes. This is why every parish (*freguesia*) in Madeira that keeps a name of a religious character takes it from a chapel that already existed and was later turned into a parish church. The same is true of the parish of Prazeres (‘joys’), whose name comes from a small chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres (Our Lady of Delights), built there long before the parish was created. It is to be presumed that the original chapel was known as the chapel of Prazeres, and that this name, thus simplified, became that of the new parish.

before: The land that makes up the greater part of the parish of Prazeres originally belonged to the parish of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’). It was detached from that parish to form, together with a few hamlets of Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’), an independent parish, created by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 28 December 1676. It was only around 1684 that the new parish was established, with its seat in the chapel of Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres. Its parish priests were Father Manuel Dias Pinheiro (1684–1692), Francisco Correia da Silva (1692–1693) and José Cordeiro de Andrade (1693–1700). In that year, 1700, the parish of Prazeres was abolished, or at least part of the parish services held there was suspended and transferred to the church of Estreito da Calheta, to whose parish the hamlets of Prazeres were annexed. We have not discovered the reasons behind this measure, which seems strange to us but did in fact take place. The locality did, however, have a chaplain of its own, who celebrated some acts of worship there.
