before: It was the chapel of São Pedro (St Peter), about whose founder and year of construction we have no information, that served as the seat of the new parish. It underwent enlargements and rebuildings in years we cannot specify. Its reconstruction was ordered by a warrant of the Treasury Council (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 20 July 1620, the works being estimated at 2,231,606 *réis*; it is not known whether the rebuilding was carried out immediately, which did not always happen. In 1851 major repairs were made to this church, at a cost of about 1,700,000 *réis*. We are informed that the parish church, through its successive constructions and reconstructions, has occupied three different places, though always within the same locality of Salão (‘hall’). It stood first at the spot called Pé do Pico (‘foot of the peak’), then at Achada da Igreja (‘church plateau’), and finally where it stands today.

before: The Ilhéu de Fora (‘outer islet’), where the lighthouse stands, is considered part of the Ponta (‘point’), although it is separated from the neighbouring land by a channel, or *boqueirão*, about 85 *braças* wide and 3 to 4 deep. To the west lie the Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros (‘islet of the landing places’) and the Ilhéu do Agostinho, followed by the bay of Abra (‘bay’), where there is a quay (see that entry), and then the locality (*sítio*) of Piedade (‘pity’), with a beach of calcareous sand, the only one of its kind on the island. On a small mound beside the beach stands the little chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity) (see that entry).

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), with 105 *foros* and 651 inhabitants. There was once a chapel there dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Fé (Our Lady of Faith), founded in 1826 by the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Diogo Dias de Orneias e Vasconcelos. There was also a chapel there dedicated to Santo António (St Anthony of Padua), belonging to the Nunes Caldeira family and founded around 1760. This locality belonged to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by the Genoese João Baptista of the Italian Usodimare family, who married a child of the first donatary (*donatário*) of Machico, Tristão Vaz Teixeira; its last representative was João Bettencourt Baptista.

before: The chapel of Senhor Bom Jesus was the centre of an ancient pilgrimage, which is still today one of the best attended on the whole island. It is recorded as already taking place in 1577, which makes it the oldest pilgrimage festival held here in Madeira. The pilgrimages of the Lord Jesus of Ponta Delgada, of Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of the Mount) and of the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*) at Machico are the oldest, the best attended and the most characteristic of this diocese.

before: This parish has the Chapel of Reis Magos (Three Kings), which belonged to the house of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’). There was formerly a chapel of Santo António at the locality of Pico (‘peak’), and another at the locality of Ladrilhos (‘tiles’); we shall deal with these elsewhere in this work.

before: In the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence) there was a chapel dedicated to the martyr St Lawrence. It is quite old and already existed in 1566, the year in which French corsairs sacked the city. It had its own chaplain, and the oldest royal decree (*alvará*) we have found appointing that chaplain is dated 15 November 1641. We have seen somewhere that on 3 October 1846 Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro ordered an inventory of the silver objects belonging to this chapel, which weighed 36 pounds, and had them deposited in the Central Treasury. A new inventory was made on 3 December 1856, with further pieces added, the whole weighing 65 pounds of silver. In 1856 the chapel’s vestments were given to the church of Achadas da Cruz (see the São Lourenço Palace).

before: The chapel of São Lourenço in the locality (*sítio*) of the same name in the parish (*freguesia*) of Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’) is quite old, for in the first years of the 16th century it was already the seat of a chaplaincy (capelania), which later became a parish. It served as the parish church until the middle of the 18th century, when the new church was built. An old tradition records that this chapel belonged to the Afonsos Jardins, who were among the earliest settlers there and owners of the *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) on which the chapel stands.

before: In the parish of Camacha there was a chapel dedicated to São Lourenço, said to have been built by Francisco Gonçalves Salgado. It was of quite old construction, and in 1676 the seat of the new parish was established in it, so that it became the parish church; its patron saint is still that of the original chapel.

before: Four months after Luís Mousinho’s arrival on this island, that is, around the middle of December 1834, the new charitable establishment began to operate. It was provisionally housed in some of the outbuildings of the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace), under the direct supervision and the solicitous and loving direction of its founders themselves. It came to shelter 120 children and remained in a state of relative prosperity for as long as its founders stayed on this island. It was still thanks to that initial impetus that, by a ministerial order (*portaria*) of 13 January 1836, a house in the Campo da Barca (‘boat field’) belonging to the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*) was obtained for the asylum to move into. It operated there for some years and ceased to exist at a date we cannot establish with complete accuracy. After the departure of Luís Mousinho de Albuquerque and his devoted and charitable wife, the work they had created with such dedication and affection began slowly to decline, until it died out completely, leaving behind only the blessed memory of its illustrious founders.

before: Gonçalo Fernandes, a mysterious figure mentioned in the old Madeiran chronicles, of whom we shall speak in a separate article, had a residence and a *sesmaria* in this parish. The parish has the chapels of Nossa Senhora do Loreto (Our Lady of Loreto), Nossa Senhora da Nazaré (Our Lady of Nazaré), the Sacred Heart of Jesus (*Sagrado Coração de Jesus*), Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*) and Nossa Senhora da Vida. Of the old chapels of Our Lady of the Flight into Egypt (*Nossa Senhora do Desterro*) and Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora only a few heaps of rubble remain today. Other chapels once existed that have vanished completely: those of Our Lady of Ransom (*Nossa Senhora das Mercês*), Our Lady of Consolation (*Nossa Senhora da Consolação*), Nossa Senhora da Visitação, Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, Santo António and Santa Maria Madalena.

before: Writing about the chantry (capela) of this dedication, Dr Álvaro de Azevedo states that it was founded by Simão de Nobrega in Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’), which is plainly a mistake. This chantry stood in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António and was built by Second Lieutenant Simão de Nobrega e Sousa and his wife Maria Tavares de Sousa on the *quinta* (country estate) they owned in the locality (*sítio*) of Pico do Cardo (‘thistle peak’), in that parish. In Curral das Freiras there was only the chapel of Santo António (St Anthony of Padua), which the nuns of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) had built. The chantry of Santa Quitéria was built in 1727, and its deed of endowment is dated 3 July of that year. By 1814 it had been deconsecrated, and divine worship had not been celebrated in it for many years. It gave its name to the locality in which it was built.

before: On the coast of the town (*vila*) of this name there is a small landing place where disembarking is difficult. The landing place at Fajã da Areia (see that entry), about two kilometres from the landing place of São Vicente, is preferable.

before: When the Funchal Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-Cirúrgica do Funchal*) was founded in 1837, Dr Luiz Henriques was appointed professor (*lente*) there and its first director. He held both posts until 1845, while also serving as chief surgeon of the Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal).

before: A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’). It has a small house that can shelter those passing through, and it is also where the waters of the Levada da Serra (‘upland channel’), which irrigates the parishes of Caniço, São Gonçalo and Santa Maria Maior, are separated into their own channel. As far as Lombo da Raiz (‘root ridge’) these waters run together with those of the Levada do Juncal (‘rush-bed channel’), destined for the parishes of Santo da Serra, Água de Pena and Santa Cruz, and with those of the Levada Nova do Furado (‘new channel of the tunnel’), which waters the lands of the parish of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’).

before: New church of São Martinho (St Martin of Tours): ‘Nossa Senhora da Incarnação’ (Our Lady of the Incarnation), ‘Nativity’ and ‘St Joachim’, a triptych, first third of the 16th century, Netherlandish School.

before: An officer of the 6th Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) battalion who was murdered at the Quartel do Colégio (College Barracks) by soldiers of that battalion on 31 July 1852. It is said that the mutineers actually meant to kill the commander, but the lieutenant stood up to them. This gave a quartermaster-sergeant (*furriel*) time to shut the door through which the soldiery had to pass to reach the commander’s room, and gave the commander, warned of what was happening, time to flee.

before: From 19 January 1896 until 27 October 1910 this was the name of the road between the parish church of Santo António (St Anthony of Padua) and the Ribeira (‘stream’). Commander Luís de Bettencourt Miranda was born in Funchal on 16 December 1856 and died there on 17 July 1921. For more than 30 years he served first as an official and then as secretary of the Council, posts in which he rendered excellent service to the municipality.

before: In the locality (*sítio*) of this name in the parish (*freguesia*) of Quinta Grande (‘large estate’), on the *quinta* (country estate) of Pombal, stands the chapel of Santo António (St Anthony of Padua). before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Roque (‘St Roch’), Funchal. In this locality, on the right bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s stream’), stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Rosário (Our Lady of the Rosary), built by João da Paz de Castro in 1668. The Jesuits had a residence there, with a private chapel and surrounding land.

before: This was the name given to the procession held on Ash Wednesday, which in distant times set out from the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi), accompanied by friars who sang religious chants along the way. The procession always passed through the churches of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) and the Mercês, where the nuns sang religious hymns as the processional litter (*andor*) bearing the image of St Francis embracing that of Christ entered the church.

before: After the church of São Francisco disappeared, the images that had featured in the Ash Wednesday procession passed to the church of the College (Igreja do Colégio, the Jesuit college church), and in our own day it was from this church that the procession set out; it has not been held for about 25 years (1921). The capes (*opas*) worn in the procession were purple, and in olden times the professed brethren who joined it wore the habit. The place of the women penitents who accompanied the cortège was near the so-called tree of penance.

before: At the council meeting of 13 November 1932 the Municipal Services (*Serviços Municipalizados*) were created, charged in particular with overseeing the sanitation works and the distribution of drinking water to homes. The tender for the award of the contract for the pipework in the middle and upper parts of the city twice attracted no bidders, so the Municipal Services took on these works themselves, estimated at 552,259.00 escudos, ‘a short section fed by a siphon to be built in the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) still remaining to be completed’, and 3,700 metres of piping having already been laid.

before: The family descends from Simão de Nóbrega, who founded the chapel of Santa Quitéria (St Quiteria) in Santo António (‘St Anthony’). In the time of the fifth captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*), Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, there lived in Madeira a certain Gaspar de Nóbrega, who was *ouvidor* (judicial officer of the donatary or the Crown) and lieutenant to that same donatary, and he may have given rise to another branch of the same family.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’). It takes its name from a chapel that once stood there, dedicated to Nossa Senhora do Livramento (Our Lady of Deliverance), which was the centre of a well-attended pilgrimage, now transferred to the parish church. The foundation of this chapel is attributed to Sebastião de Oliveira, around the middle of the 17th century; he held land there as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation).

before: This distinguished writer and journalist, who died in 1915, visited this island several times and held the most devoted admiration for its natural beauty and mild climate. It was in 1913, when he spent a long stay in this city, that he argued brilliantly and with weighty arguments for the idea of rebuilding the house where Christopher Columbus lived, as we have mentioned elsewhere (vol. 1, p. 286 ff.). He also concerned himself with the triptych painted on wood in the sacristy of the parish church of São Pedro (St Peter), making known to Madeirans the fine description of it by the distinguished writer Manuel Teixeira Gomes in his book *Cartas sem moral nenhuma*.

before: On a visit to Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’) he made some botanical collections there, and his petrological collections from the archipelago are among the most complete known. before: In this locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Nossa Senhora do Monte (‘Our Lady of the Mount’) stand the parish church dedicated to this patron saint, where Emperor Charles of Austria lies buried – he died at the *quinta* (country estate) of Monte on 1 April 1922 – and the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception), founded a few years ago by Captain José Sotero da Silva and today the property of José de Freitas Belmonte.

before: Caminho Grande (‘main road’) or Preces, a locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’). Here stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Preces (Our Lady of Prayers), which gave the place its name; it was founded in 1683 by Father Francisco da Cunha e Mendonça. In the same locality is the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Nazaré (Our Lady of Nazaré), built in 1757 by Dona Maria do Rosário Henriques, widow of Pedro Bernardes Cordeiro. At the place known as Fonte da Rocha (‘rock spring’), the ruins can still be seen of an old chapel dedicated to São Cândido (St Candidus), which Canon Francisco Cândido Correia Henriques had built in 1732. It has 96 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) and 516 inhabitants.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), taking in part of the cluster of houses around the small cove. It is the seat of the municipality (*concelho*), and here are the town hall, various public offices, the post and telegraph office, the parish church and the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception). This place was never raised to the rank of town (*vila*), although it is commonly called one, even in official documents (see the articles headed Câmara de Lobos).

before: The patron saint of this parish was Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity) until 1744, when it became St Joseph, at the time the new church was built. By the papal briefs of 24 and 26 August 1784 the altar of the chancel was declared a privileged altar, and a plenary indulgence was granted, to be gained on the feast of St Joseph. We have found somewhere the curious information that the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Francisco Aurélio da Câmara Leme charged the third of his estate with a perpetual obligation to supply the oil needed to light the Blessed Sacrament in the church of Arco de São Jorge. His son and heir, the holder of the entail Francisco António da Câmara Leme, ratified and took on this obligation by a public deed executed on 18 February 1766, the charge falling ‘on the *quinta* (country estate) before Santo Amaro’.

before: Old Madeiran books of genealogy say that Afonso Álvares Columbreiro, a native of a settlement on the outskirts of Seville, was one of the first and noble settlers of the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’). They add that he founded there the chantries (capela) of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria) and São Bento (St Benedict of Nursia) within the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he had established, whose seat lay in that parish (*freguesia*). One of his granddaughters, named Brígida Gonçalves, and her husband João Mealheiro or Malheiro, who held the rank of noblemen, were the ancestors of Father Manuel Álvares. He therefore came of noble lineage, which in any case adds little to his undeniable merits and virtues. His parents were Sebastião Gonçalves and Beatriz Álvares, who retained the privileges of nobility inherited from their forebears.

before: The procession of the Litanies (*Ladainhas*, a Rogation procession) took place in May. before: In 1607 the Council ordered that on the first day the same procession should go to the chapel of Espírito Santo, on the second to that of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Jangão?) and on the third to that of São Sebastião. before: The chancel, which Dr Álvaro de Azevedo says bears the decadent, hybrid stamp of the 17th century, is entirely out of keeping with the dominant style of the whole church, as are the sacristy and the chapel of the Santíssimo Sacramento (Blessed Sacrament). The harmony of the original style was broken still further by the major repairs carried out after the earthquake of 1748, which caused considerable damage there, just as the French had already done irreparable harm in 1566. At the end of the 18th century, Canon João Paulo had several altars that were in an advanced state of ruin rebuilt at his own expense. He also had the present windows of the main façade opened; they contrast sharply with the pointed doorway and the rose window above, and robbed that frontispiece of the pure lines of the Manueline style that had been its own.

before: It is on 7 January, after Epiphany, that the *lapinhas* (Madeiran Christmas crib) are taken down and everything returns to normal. Some people, however, keep their nativity scenes set up until the 15th, the feast of Santo Amaro (St Maurus), which, in the opinion of some, is when the Christmas festivities so dear to the good people of Madeira should be considered over. See Lapinha.

before: A former locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), corresponding roughly to the site now occupied by the Monte Palace Hotel and its surroundings. A chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres (Our Lady of the Seven Joys) once stood here and gave the place its name.

before: The locality of Lamaceiros (‘mud flats’) in Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) is also worth a visit. From some nearby peaks part of the Ribeira da Janela (‘window stream’) can be seen. There is a chapel there dedicated to São Pedro (St Peter), badly damaged by the earthquake of 1748 and rebuilt shortly afterwards; it was restored once again a few years ago.

before: The parish (*freguesia*) took its name from the small chapel of São Roque (St Roch) that stood there, where the seat of the new parish was established. The chapel had been built by the inhabitants of the locality (*sítio*) in a year before the parish was created. Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, basing himself on the order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 19 May 1704, which directed that the building of the new church and sacristy be put out to award by public auction (*arrematação*) for the sum of 795,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), appears to conclude that the present church was built in that year. This construction, or rather enlargement, was carried out on the chapel that stood in the locality still known today as Igreja Paroquial (‘parish church’), which we believe to be the site of the original chapel of São Roque. The work seems to have been none too sound, for around 1790 the church collapsed and could no longer be used for worship. Religious services were then held in a small chapel whose dedication we do not know.

before: The royal decree (alvará régio) of Cardinal Henry the Navigator, dated 3 March 1579, empowered the diocesan prelate Dom Jerónimo Barreto to create the parish of São Roque, and set the parish priest’s annual stipend (*côngrua*) at 14,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash, half a *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and a quarter of wine. The royal decree of 16 January 1589 raised this salary to 19,000 *réis* in cash, half a *moio* of wheat and a quarter of wine, to which the decree of the 30th of the same month and year added a further 3,000 *réis* in cash and half a *moio* of wheat.

before: Before it acquired the magnificent building facing the Largo do Município, or Largo do Colégio (the College), the Council met in various parts of Funchal. The first building it owned, though not the first in which it held its meetings, was built under an order of Duke Manuel I dated 1486, which directed that a ‘stronghold, council chamber, notaries’ house & pillory’ be built on the square called the Campo do Duque (‘duke’s field’), the ground on which the Cathedral (the Sé) and its adjoining squares and streets now stand. As early as 1470 a letter from Infante Ferdinand to the donatary João Gonçalves da Câmara had asked him to undertake ‘to build the council house & the council pound’ out of the money from the fines of the judge-auditor & of João Gonçalves himself’. The same Infante ordered land to be given beside the great church for this building, which was estimated at 213,096 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis).
